Attribute Randomization Sensitivity TestMONTE CARLO

sensitivity_test
Monte Carlo permutation test that assesses whether an observed Global Moran's I could have arisen by chance. The observed $I$ is compared against a reference distribution of $I$ values generated by randomly shuffling attribute values across features (breaking any real spatial structure while preserving the marginal distribution of the variable and the fixed spatial configuration). This technique, rooted in the randomization inference framework of Fisher (1935) and extended to spatial data by Cliff & Ord (1981), constructs the sampling distribution empirically rather than relying on asymptotic normality assumptions. The test produces an HTML report containing the observed $I$, the simulation reference distribution (visualized as an inline SVG histogram), an empirical pseudo-p-value, a sensitivity verdict with color-coded confidence level, and context-sensitive analyst-action recommendations. Pure NumPy implementation — no external packages required.
Display Equations
1. Observed Global Moran's I. The test statistic computed from the actual spatial arrangement of attribute values:
$$I_{\text{obs}} = \frac{n}{S_0} \cdot \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{ij} (x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad S_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{ij}$$ where $w_{ij}$ is the spatial weight between features $i$ and $j$ (binary distance-band weights with $w_{ii} = 0$).
2. Permutation Mechanism. In each simulation $s$, the attribute values are randomly permuted across the fixed spatial locations while preserving the weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$:
$$\mathbf{x}^{(s)} = \pi_s(\mathbf{x}), \qquad I_{\text{sim}}^{(s)} = \frac{n}{S_0} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{z}^{(s)\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{z}^{(s)}}{\mathbf{z}^{(s)\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{z}^{(s)}}$$ where $\pi_s$ is a random permutation of the $n$ indices and $\mathbf{z}^{(s)} = \mathbf{x}^{(s)} - \bar{x}^{(s)} \mathbf{1}$.
3. Reference Distribution and Empirical p-value. After $M$ simulations, the empirical two-tailed p-value is computed as:
$$p_{\text{emp}} = \frac{\sum_{s=1}^{M} \mathbb{I}\bigl(|I_{\text{sim}}^{(s)}| \geq |I_{\text{obs}}|\bigr) + 1}{M + 1}$$ The addition of 1 to numerator and denominator (the Davison & Hinkley correction) ensures that $p_{\text{emp}} \gt 0$ and avoids degenerate p-values when $M$ is small. For $M = 999$, the minimum achievable p-value is $1/1000 = 0.001$.
4. Simulation Moments. The simulated mean and standard deviation characterize the reference distribution:
$$\bar{I}_{\text{sim}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{s=1}^{M} I_{\text{sim}}^{(s)}, \qquad \sigma_{\text{sim}} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{M-1} \sum_{s=1}^{M} \bigl( I_{\text{sim}}^{(s)} - \bar{I}_{\text{sim}} \bigr)^2 }$$ Under the null hypothesis of random spatial arrangement, $\bar{I}_{\text{sim}} \approx E(I) = -1/(n-1)$.
5. Percentile-Based Confidence Bounds. The 90% reference interval is:
$$\bigl[ I_{[0.05]}^{\text{sim}}, \; I_{[0.95]}^{\text{sim}} \bigr]$$ where $I_{[q]}^{\text{sim}}$ denotes the $q$-th empirical quantile of the simulated $I$ values. If $I_{\text{obs}}$ lies outside this interval, the spatial pattern is robust at $\alpha = 0.10$ (two-tailed).
6. Sensitivity Verdict Logic. The verdict is determined by the empirical p-value against conventional significance thresholds:
$$\text{Verdict} = \begin{cases} \text{ROBUST} & p_{\text{emp}} \lt 0.05 \\ \text{SENSITIVE} & p_{\text{emp}} \geq 0.05 \end{cases}$$ ROBUST: The observed spatial structure is unlikely under random reassignment of attribute values — the pattern is statistically defensible for this neighborhood definition.
SENSITIVE: The observed pattern falls within the range expected from random attribute arrangements — the apparent clustering is not robust enough to treat as planning evidence without additional verification.
7. Neighborhood Topology Diagnostics. The sensitivity result is qualified by the neighborhood graph structure. Key diagnostics include:
$$n_{\text{isolated}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{I}\!\left( \sum_{j} w_{ij} = 0 \right), \qquad d_{\text{density}} = \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}}{n(n-1)}$$ where $n_{\text{isolated}}$ is the count of features with zero neighbors (requires distance-band increase) and $d_{\text{density}}$ is the graph density (high density risks over-smoothing).
Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Input vector layer (any geometry; centroids used for distance computation)
FIELDNumeric Field—Target variable for sensitivity assessment. Must have variation (non-constant); non-numeric or NULL values are skipped with a diagnostic count
DISTANCE_BANDDouble1000.0Distance threshold in map units for spatial-weight construction. Features within this distance are neighbors. Use Calculate Distance Band (Group 01) or Incremental Autocorrelation (Group 02) to determine a data-driven threshold
SIMULATIONSInteger999Number of Monte Carlo permutations (99–9999). Higher values produce more stable p-values: 999 is standard, 9999 recommended for publication-quality inference. Runtime scales linearly with simulation count
HTML_REPORTFile (HTML)—Output sensitivity report: verdict box, observed vs. simulated statistics table, inline SVG histogram of reference distribution with observed-I marker, diagnostic tables (numeric quality, neighborhood topology, CRS warning), sensitivity cautions, recommended next action, and methodological caveats
HTML Report Diagnostics
Header — attribute name, feature count, distance band, simulation count, skipped-record count · Verdict box (color-coded) — ROBUST (green: $p_{\text{emp}} \lt 0.05$) or SENSITIVE (red: $p_{\text{emp}} \geq 0.05$), with a plain-language description of what the verdict means for planning evidence · Executive summary — narrative describing the test logic and scope of inference · Simulation statistics table — observed $I$, simulated mean $I$, simulated std dev, empirical p-value, 5th and 95th percentiles of the reference distribution · Numeric quality diagnostics — sample size, missing count, constant-value check, value range, mean, std dev · Neighborhood topology diagnostics — neighbor count distribution (min/median/max), isolated feature count, distance-band configuration, neighborhood density label · CRS warning (if geographic CRS detected with distance-band weights) · Inline SVG histogram — reference distribution of simulated $I$ values (20-bin histogram) with a dashed red vertical line marking the observed $I$ position · Recommended analyst action — context-sensitive: if ROBUST → "treat pattern as robust for follow-up local analysis"; if SENSITIVE → "revisit variable choice, study area, or neighborhood definition"; if isolated features present → "increase distance band before relying on result" · Sensitivity cautions — specific warnings about isolation, over-smoothing, and neighborhood definition · Methodological caveats — permutation-test assumptions, scope of inference, and comparison with analytical z-score approaches
Extended Interpretation Guide
1. ROBUST vs. SENSITIVE — what the verdict means. A ROBUST verdict means the observed spatial autocorrelation is statistically unusual given the neighborhood definition — the pattern would be unlikely to emerge from randomly relocating attribute values. This does not confirm causation or identify the generating process; it confirms that the spatial structure merits further investigation. A SENSITIVE verdict means the observed pattern could plausibly arise from random attribute assignment — the apparent clustering is not distinguishable from noise at this spatial scale. This does not mean there is no pattern; it means the evidence is insufficient.
2. The role of the distance band. The sensitivity result is conditional on the chosen distance band. A pattern that is ROBUST at one spatial scale may be SENSITIVE at another (this is what the Incremental Autocorrelation tool in Group 02 is designed to explore). Best practice: run the sensitivity test at two or three defensible distance bands (e.g., the Incremental Autocorrelation peak, half that, double that) and compare verdicts. A pattern that is ROBUST across multiple scales is stronger evidence than one that depends on a particular bandwidth.
3. Comparing empirical p-values with analytical z-scores. The analytical z-score for Moran's I (from the Global Moran's I tool in Group 02) assumes asymptotic normality of the test statistic. When the underlying variable is heavily skewed, has extreme outliers, or when $n$ is small, this assumption can be violated. The permutation test makes no distributional assumptions — it constructs the reference distribution empirically from the data itself. If the analytical z-score suggests significance (p < 0.05) but the permutation p-value does not, the analytical result may be inflated by non-normality.
4. Neighborhood topology as a diagnostic. The report flags isolated features (zero neighbors at the chosen distance band) and graph density. Isolated features reduce effective sample size and can inflate or deflate $I$ depending on their attribute values. A "Very dense" neighborhood graph means most features are mutual neighbors, which produces over-smoothed local statistics. The HTML report provides specific action guidance for both conditions.
5. From robustness to evidence. Sensitivity testing is a screening step, not a final answer. A ROBUST result justifies proceeding to local analysis (LISA, Gi*) to identify where the pattern is concentrated. A SENSITIVE result does not invalidate the variable — it suggests that (a) the spatial scale may be wrong, (b) the attribute distribution may be too noisy, or (c) the study area may be too heterogeneous to produce a detectable global pattern. In all cases, the sensitivity report provides structured evidence for the modeling workflow decision, not a binary gate.
Algorithm Implementation Notes
Engine. The sensitivity simulation is implemented in core/stats_engines.py as run_sensitivity_simulation(). The function constructs a dense $n \times n$ binary weight matrix from the distance band, computes the observed Moran's $I$ using a fast quadratic-form computation ($\mathbf{z}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}$ via NumPy), then performs $M$ random permutations of the attribute vector using numpy.random.default_rng with a fixed seed for reproducibility. Each permutation's $I$ is computed using the same fast path. The function returns the observed $I$, the full simulated distribution (as a Python list for histogram construction), and summary statistics. The verdict logic in core/sensitivity_audit.py transforms the numerical results into the color-coded verdict, cautions list, and analyst-action recommendations that appear in the HTML report.
Computational scaling. Each simulation requires one permutation and one matrix-vector product. For $n = 500$ features and $M = 999$ simulations, runtime is under one second. For $n = 5000$, runtime is approximately 5–15 seconds depending on weight-matrix density. The weight matrix is stored densely ( $n \times n$ floats), so memory usage is approximately $8n^2$ bytes (e.g., ~200 MB for $n = 5000$). For very large datasets, consider spatial subsampling before running the sensitivity test.
See also: Global Moran's I

Model Comparison Matrix

model_comparison_matrix
Automatically detects and compares multiple PlanX GeoStats model output layers (OLS, GLR, SAR, SEM, GWR, MGWR) side by side, extracting observed values, predicted values, and residuals from each model's standard diagnostic fields. Computes a unified set of comparable metrics — R², RMSE, MAE, prediction bias, record coverage, and residual spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I with p-value) — across all detected models. Ranks models using a weighted composite audit score that balances predictive accuracy, spatial specification quality, and coverage completeness. Generates a structured HTML comparison report designed to make the model-selection logic transparent, auditable, and defensible in planning reports. Pure NumPy implementation — no external packages required.
Display Equations
1. Coefficient of Determination (R²). Computed from the extracted observed and predicted values for each model:
$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \bar{y})^2}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i$$ Models with higher $R^2$ explain more variance, but $R^2$ alone is insufficient for model selection — it rewards complexity without penalizing it.
2. Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Measures prediction error in the original units of the dependent variable:
$$\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 }$$ RMSE penalizes large errors quadratically, making it sensitive to outliers. Lower RMSE indicates better predictive accuracy.
3. Mean Absolute Error (MAE). An alternative error metric less sensitive to outliers than RMSE:
$$\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl| y_i - \hat{y}_i \bigr|$$ MAE is interpretable as the average absolute deviation in the dependent variable's original units. For planning audiences, MAE is often more intuitive than RMSE.
4. Prediction Bias. The mean of residuals — a signed indicator of systematic over- or under-prediction:
$$\text{Bias} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)$$ Positive bias indicates systematic under-prediction (observed values tend to exceed predictions); negative bias indicates systematic over-prediction. A well-specified model should have bias close to zero.
5. Model Coverage. The fraction of features in the model output layer with valid predictions and residuals:
$$\text{Coverage} = \frac{n_{\text{valid}}}{N_{\text{total}}}$$ where $n_{\text{valid}}$ is the count of features with non-null observed, predicted, and residual values, and $N_{\text{total}}$ is the total feature count. Low coverage reduces comparability — models fitted on different subsets of features produce metrics on different samples.
6. Residual Spatial Autocorrelation (Moran's I on Residuals). Tests whether model residuals retain spatial structure — a key diagnostic for spatial model adequacy:
$$I_{\text{resid}} = \frac{n}{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}} \cdot \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij} (e_i - \bar{e})(e_j - \bar{e})}{\sum_i (e_i - \bar{e})^2}$$ A significant $I_{\text{resid}}$ (p < 0.05) indicates that the model specification did not fully absorb the spatial pattern in the data. Clean residuals are a hallmark of a well-specified spatial model.
7. Composite Audit Score. Models are ranked by a weighted composite score designed to balance predictive accuracy, spatial specification, and data completeness:
$$\text{Score} = 0.45 \cdot \frac{\text{RMSE}}{\max(\text{RMSE})} \;+\; 0.25 \cdot \frac{\text{MAE}}{\max(\text{MAE})} \;+\; \delta_{\text{resid}} \;+\; 0.15 \cdot (1 - \text{Coverage})$$ where the residual spatial-pattern penalty $\delta_{\text{resid}}$ is: $$\delta_{\text{resid}} = \begin{cases} 0.35 & p_{\text{resid}} \lt 0.05 \text{ (significant residual autocorrelation)} \\ 0.25 & \text{residual diagnostics unavailable} \\ 0.00 & p_{\text{resid}} \geq 0.05 \text{ (spatially clean residuals)} \end{cases}$$ Lower scores are better. A model achieving the best RMSE and MAE with clean residuals receives the lowest (best) score.
8. Recommendation Logic. The report first identifies models with clean residuals ($p_{\text{resid}} \geq 0.05$). If such models exist, the one with the lowest composite score is recommended. If no model has clean residuals, the report notes that every candidate retains residual spatial structure and recommends inspecting residual maps rather than selecting by score alone.
Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultDescription
MODEL_LAYERSMultiple Vector Layers—Select two or more PlanX GeoStats model output layers. The tool auto-detects model type from diagnostic field signatures: residual/y_predicted → GWR; mgwr_pred/mgwr_resid → MGWR; sar_pred/sar_resid → SAR; sem_pred/sem_resid → SEM; glr_fit/glr_resid → GLR; residual alone → OLS
DEP_VARNumeric Field—Observed dependent variable field name. Must exist in ALL selected layers. The tool extracts observed values from this field in each layer and pairs them with each model's predicted values for metric computation
HTML_REPORTFile (HTML)—Output comparison report: executive summary with recommendation, ranked comparison table with per-model metrics and scores, interpretation guide, and recommended analyst actions
HTML Report Diagnostics
Header — observed dependent field name, number of compared layers · Executive summary — recommendation narrative: identifies the top-scoring model with clean residuals (if any exist), or flags that all models retain spatial structure · Comparison table — one row per model, sorted by rank (best first): layer name, detected model type, rank, composite score, $n$ (valid records), coverage, $R^2$, RMSE, MAE, bias, residual Moran's $I$, residual p-value, residual status ("Clean" / "Spatial pattern" / "Not available") · Row highlighting — rows with significant residual autocorrelation are highlighted with a warning background · Unusable-layer rows — layers that lack recognized diagnostic fields are listed with a diagnostic message · Reading guide — narrative explaining how to interpret the table, the limitations of fit-only model selection, and the importance of residual diagnostics · Recommended analyst actions — four-item checklist: inspect residual clusters, verify comparable coverage, use OLS/GLR as baselines, document the final choice with theory and diagnostics
Extended Interpretation Guide
1. The composite score is a discussion aid, not a decision rule. The score aggregates RMSE, MAE, residual spatial structure, and coverage into a single number for ranking convenience. A model that ranks first by score but relies on variables that are expensive to measure, politically contentious, or theoretically unsupported should not be selected over a close second-ranked model with stronger substantive grounding. The score narrows the field; the analyst makes the call.
2. Residual spatial autocorrelation is the highest-weight diagnostic. A model can achieve excellent predictive fit (high $R^2$, low RMSE) while still leaving strong spatial structure in its residuals. This indicates that the model is capturing the non-spatial variation well but missing a spatially-organized component — possibly an omitted variable, a boundary effect, or a scale mismatch. The comparison report's residual diagnostics help identify which models are spatially well-specified versus which are merely well-fitting.
3. Coverage comparability. If models were run on the same input layer with the same dependent variable and same missing-data handling, coverage should be equal across models. Coverage differences indicate that one model excluded records that another included — for example, a spatial autoregression model might drop isolated features that a GWR model retains. When coverage differs by more than a few percent, the metrics are not strictly comparable (they describe performance on different subsets of features). The report flags this implicitly; analysts should verify comparable coverage before drawing conclusions.
4. The role of model complexity. The composite score does not include a direct complexity penalty beyond what is implicit in the residual spatial-pattern penalty (more complex spatial models should produce cleaner residuals if the added complexity is warranted). For a formal complexity-penalized comparison, use AICc from each model's individual HTML report. The Comparison Matrix complements AICc-based selection with error-metric and diagnostic perspectives that AICc alone does not provide.
5. From comparison to reporting. After selecting a model, document: (a) why this model class (OLS, GWR, MGWR, SAR, SEM) is appropriate for the planning question, (b) which variables were included and why, (c) the spatial weights specification (queen/rook/KNN/distance-band), (d) the key diagnostic results (RMSE, residual Moran's I, and local diagnostics if applicable), and (e) the limitations acknowledged. The comparison report provides all of this evidence in a structured, reproducible format suitable for inclusion in a planning report appendix.

Algorithm Implementation Notes
Engine. Model comparison is implemented in algorithms/alg_model_comparison.py. The algorithm iterates over each selected layer, detects its model type by checking for the diagnostic field signatures defined in MODEL_SPECS, extracts observed ($y_i$), predicted ($\hat{y}_i$), and residual ($e_i$) values for all valid features (skipping features marked as unused via the model-specific flag field), computes fit metrics via core/analysis_diagnostics.model_fit_summary(), builds spatial weights for residual autocorrelation testing (Queen for polygons, KNN=8 for points/lines), and computes residual Moran's I via residual_spatial_autocorrelation_summary(). Composite scores are assigned by core/model_audit.assign_model_scores(), which normalizes RMSE and MAE by their maximum values, adds the residual-pattern penalty, and adds a coverage penalty. The recommendation text is generated by model_recommendation(), which prioritizes models with clean residuals when they exist.
Computational scaling. The tool reads each layer's attribute table (I/O-bound), computes fit metrics (trivial), and runs residual spatial autocorrelation diagnostics (requires spatial-weight construction per layer). For layers with thousands of features, weight construction dominates runtime. For $k$ layers each with $n \approx 1000$ features, total runtime is a few seconds. The comparison tool is designed to be run interactively as the final step in a modeling session.

Spatial Regime Regression

spatial_regime_regression
Fits a separate intercept and full coefficient set for every distinct value of a categorical regime field (districts, zoning categories, any partition of the study area), then tests with a Chow test whether that structural split is statistically justified over one pooled model. Wraps spreg.OLS_Regimes from the PySAL spreg package.
1. Theoretical Background

Structural instability, not just a shifted intercept. Including a categorical field as an ordinary dummy variable in OLS only lets the regime shift the average outcome (the intercept) — it forces every explanatory field to keep the same slope everywhere. Spatial regime regression, following the "regimes" framework developed within the PySAL spreg ecosystem (Anselin, 1988, 1990), instead estimates a fully separate model per regime: every coefficient, not just the intercept, is allowed to differ. This answers a stronger and often more realistic planning question — not "does this district have a higher baseline outcome" but "does the whole relationship between the explanatory fields and the outcome work differently in this district."

The Chow test as the arbiter. Chow (1960) formalized the test this tool reports: an F-type statistic comparing the fit of separate regime-specific models against one pooled model, under the null hypothesis that the true coefficients are identical across regimes. A significant Chow test is the formal justification for reporting per-regime coefficients at all — without it, the apparent differences between regimes could easily be sampling noise, and a single pooled Generalized Linear Regression model is both simpler and equally defensible.

Spatial heterogeneity versus spatial dependence. Anselin (1988, 1990) draws a foundational distinction between two ways space can matter in a regression: spatial dependence (nearby observations' error terms or outcomes are correlated — the concern GWR, Spatial Lag, and Spatial Error address) and spatial heterogeneity (the relationship itself differs by location or group). Spatial regimes address heterogeneity directly, using a discrete, analyst-defined partition rather than a continuous surface — the regime field can be a genuinely spatial partition (north/south halves, planning districts) or any other categorical grouping the analyst believes changes the underlying process, which is why the method sits in the "Models and Scenarios" group rather than requiring a spatial-weights matrix the way SAR/SEM/SDM do.

Regimes versus GWR — a discrete-versus-continuous choice. GWR (this group) also lets coefficients vary spatially, but continuously and smoothly via a kernel bandwidth, producing one local coefficient surface per explanatory field rather than a handful of regime-specific tables. Choose Spatial Regime Regression when there is a real, defensible discrete boundary (an administrative district, a zoning category, a before/after policy split) that plausibly changes the whole model at once; choose GWR when spatial variation is expected to be gradual and no single partition captures it well. The two are not mutually exclusive checks — running both and comparing whether GWR's local coefficients shift sharply near the proposed regime boundaries is itself informative about whether the discrete partition is a reasonable simplification.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Let \(r \in \{1, \dots, R\}\) index the regimes and \(n_r\) the number of complete records in regime r.

Per-regime model (constant_regi="many", cols2regi="all" — this tool's fixed specification):

$$y_i = \beta_{0,r(i)} + \sum_{k=1}^{p} \beta_{k,r(i)}\, x_{ik} + \varepsilon_i \tag{1}$$

Pooled (null) model:

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{p} \beta_k\, x_{ik} + \varepsilon_i \tag{2}$$

Chow (joint) test statistic:

$$F = \frac{(RSS_{\text{pooled}} - RSS_{\text{regimes}}) / [(R-1)(p+1)]}{RSS_{\text{regimes}} / (n - R(p+1))} \tag{3}$$

Per-regime \(R^2\) (fit quality within regime \(r\) alone, useful alongside the joint test):

$$R^2_r = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i \in r}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_{i \in r}(y_i - \bar{y}_r)^2} \tag{4}$$
Implementation note. The algorithm (algorithms/alg_spatial_regime_regression.py) extracts complete records per regime, warns when any regime has too few records to estimate its own coefficients reliably (\(n_r \le p+2\)), and delegates fitting entirely to spreg.OLS_Regimes — no regime-splitting logic is reimplemented locally. Coefficient and Chow-test values are read defensively via getattr with fallbacks, since exact attribute names have shifted slightly across spreg releases; a version mismatch surfaces as a clear error naming the missing attribute rather than a silent wrong number.

REGIME_FIELDAny Field—≥ 2 distinct valuesCategorical field defining the regimes

5. Interpretation Guide
Reading the Chow test. p < 0.05 on the joint Chow test means the regimes genuinely behave differently and the per-regime coefficient tables are worth reporting. p ≥ 0.05 means a single pooled Generalized Linear Regression model is simpler and just as defensible — do not present per-regime coefficients as meaningfully different without this test backing them up. Regimes with very few complete records will show wide, unstable coefficients regardless of the overall test result; check per-regime record counts (printed to the Processing log) before trusting any single regime's numbers.

Choosing the regime field. The strongest regime candidates are ones with an a priori theoretical reason to expect structural difference — a zoning boundary that changes what can legally be built, an administrative border with different service levels, a clear before/after policy date — rather than an arbitrary post-hoc split chosen because it happens to look different in the data. If several candidate regime fields are available, prefer the one motivated by planning theory over the one that happens to maximize the Chow F-statistic; testing several candidates and reporting only the significant one invites the same multiple-comparisons problem as p-hacking in any other statistical setting.

See also: Generalized Linear Regression · Model Comparison Matrix · GWR · MGWR

Quantile Regression

quantile_regression
Fits a linear model for one conditional quantile (Tau) of the dependent variable rather than its conditional mean, via iteratively reweighted least squares on the pinball loss — no optional dependency required. At Tau=0.5 this is median regression; at any other Tau it describes what drives that specific part of the outcome distribution, which can genuinely differ from what drives the average case.
1. Theoretical Background

Origins. Koenker and Bassett (1978) introduced quantile regression as a generalization of the sample median's robustness to the full conditional distribution: instead of minimizing squared error (which estimates the conditional mean), quantile regression minimizes an asymmetric "pinball" loss that estimates any chosen conditional quantile. For skewed planning outcomes — housing prices, permit-processing times, traffic counts — the factors that drive the median case and the factors that drive the upper tail are frequently different, a distinction OLS cannot see because it only ever estimates the mean.

Why IRLS instead of the classical LP solver. The reference algorithm for quantile regression is a linear program (Koenker & Bassett's original simplex-based method, later Barrodale-Roberts and interior-point variants). This tool instead uses an iteratively reweighted least squares scheme in the tradition of Schlossmacher's (1973) algorithm for L1 regression: each iteration re-weights every observation by \(\tau/|r_i|\) or \((1-\tau)/|r_i|\) depending on the residual's sign, then re-solves ordinary weighted least squares. This converges to the same solution as the LP formulation for well-behaved data while needing no external optimization library — consistent with this plugin's native-NumPy-first approach for tools that do not strictly require a heavier dependency.

Why this matters specifically for planning equity questions. Koenker and Hallock (2001) popularized quantile regression in applied economics precisely because so many policy-relevant outcomes are about distributional tails, not averages: a housing-affordability program cares about the lower tail of income relative to housing cost, an emergency-response standard cares about the upper tail of response time, and a permit-backlog policy cares about the worst-case processing time, not the mean. A model that only ever reports the conditional mean effect can be systematically uninformative about exactly the part of the distribution a planning intervention is meant to target.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Pinball (check) loss minimized by the Tau-quantile fit:

$$\rho_\tau(r) = r\big(\tau - \mathbb{1}[r < 0]\big) \tag{1}$$

IRLS weight at each iteration (residual \(r_i = y_i - x_i'\beta\)):

$$w_i = \frac{\tau\,\mathbb{1}[r_i \ge 0] + (1-\tau)\,\mathbb{1}[r_i < 0]}{\max(|r_i|,\, \epsilon)} \tag{2}$$

Weighted least squares update:

$$\hat{\beta}^{(t+1)} = (X'W^{(t)}X)^{-1}X'W^{(t)}y \tag{3}$$

Pseudo-\(R^2\) (Koenker & Machado 1999, R1):

$$R^2_1 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i \rho_\tau(y_i - \hat{y}_i)}{\sum_i \rho_\tau(y_i - Q_\tau(y))} \tag{4}$$

Unconditional quantile of \(y\) used as the null-model benchmark in equation 4:

$$Q_\tau(y) = \arg\min_{q} \sum_i \rho_\tau(y_i - q) \tag{5}$$
Implementation note. The engine (core/stats_engines.py::calculate_quantile_regression) initializes from the OLS solution and iterates the reweighting scheme above to a coefficient-change tolerance of \(10^{-6}\) (default 100 iterations). No standard errors or p-values are produced — proper quantile-regression inference needs bootstrap or sandwich-estimator methods outside this tool's scope — so the report shows coefficients and the pseudo-\(R^2\) only, and documents that limitation explicitly rather than presenting an incomplete inference table.
3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription

INDEPENDENTSNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldExplanatory variable fields
TAUDouble0.50.01–0.99Target conditional quantile
OUTPUTVector Layer——Output predictions layer
4. Output Description
FieldTypeDescription
qr_fitDoubleFitted Tau-quantile value
qr_residDoubleObserved minus fitted
qr_usedInteger1 if the record had complete values and was used, 0 otherwise
5. Interpretation Guide
Read across Tau values, not one run alone. Run this tool at Tau=0.1, 0.5, and 0.9 on the same fields and compare coefficients: a field with a small, stable coefficient across all three is a genuinely constant driver; a field whose coefficient grows sharply at Tau=0.9 is specifically driving the upper tail. Coefficients describe association with the chosen quantile, not the mean — never mix them with OLS coefficients in the same sentence without naming which quantile they refer to. No significance testing is available here; treat coefficients descriptively.

Quantile crossing. Because each Tau is fit as an independent run rather than jointly, fitted values at a higher Tau are not mathematically guaranteed to exceed those at a lower Tau for every record (a well-known quantile-regression phenomenon called "crossing"). This is rarely severe with well-behaved planning data and a handful of Tau values, but if fitted qr_fit values from a Tau=0.75 run come out below a Tau=0.5 run for the same records, treat both fits as approximate near that inconsistency rather than trusting either precisely.

See also: Generalized Linear Regression · OLS Regression

Koenker, R. & Hallock, K.F. (2001). "Quantile Regression." Journal of Economic Perspectives 15(4): 143–156. DOI: 10.1257/jep.15.4.143 — Widely cited accessible overview motivating quantile regression for distributional policy questions.

Koenker, R. & Machado, J.A.F. (1999). "Goodness of Fit and Related Inference Processes for Quantile Regression." Journal of the American Statistical Association 94(448): 1296–1310. DOI: 10.1080/01621459.1999.10473882 — Source of the R1 pseudo-\(R^2\) this tool reports.

Geographically Weighted Summary Statistics

gw_summary_statistics
Computes a local, kernel-weighted mean, standard deviation, and skewness of one numeric field at every feature — a spatial analog of a rolling average, using the same Fixed Gaussian / Fixed Bisquare / Adaptive Bisquare kernel families as GWR and MGWR so bandwidth intuition carries over directly.
1. Theoretical Background

Local statistics as an exploratory complement to local regression. Geographically weighted regression (Brunsdon, Fotheringham & Charlton, 1996) replaced a single global regression coefficient with a smoothly varying local surface of coefficients. The same kernel-weighting machinery, applied to plain summary statistics instead of a regression fit, answers a simpler but equally useful question: "what does this field look like around here" — a spatial analog of a rolling average that reveals variance and skewness patterns a single global mean/std entirely hides.

Effective sample size, not just a weighted average. Because kernel weights taper smoothly to zero rather than cutting off sharply, a naive count of "how many points are in the window" is not meaningful. This tool instead reports the Kish (1965) effective sample size, \(n_{\text{eff}} = (\sum w_i)^2 / \sum w_i^2\) — a standard survey-statistics device for expressing how many equally-weighted observations a set of unequal weights is worth. A low \(n_{\text{eff}}\) flags a local estimate resting on very little effective information, even if many points technically fall within a wide kernel's tail.

Precedent in the GWR software ecosystem. Geographically weighted descriptive statistics are not a novel idea invented for this plugin — the widely used GWmodel R package (Gollini et al., 2015; building on Brunsdon, Fotheringham & Charlton's original GWR software) ships a dedicated gwss() function computing local mean, standard deviation, skewness, and correlation, precisely to give analysts an exploratory, model-free first look at spatial non-stationarity before committing to a full local regression. This tool follows the same logic: run it before GWR/MGWR to see whether a field's spread genuinely varies enough across the study area to justify the heavier local-regression machinery, not only after.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Local weighted mean at location \(i\):

$$\bar{v}_i = \frac{\sum_j w_{ij}\, v_j}{\sum_j w_{ij}} \tag{1}$$

Local weighted standard deviation and skewness:

$$s_i = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_j w_{ij}(v_j - \bar{v}_i)^2}{\sum_j w_{ij}}}, \qquad \text{skew}_i = \frac{\sum_j w_{ij}(v_j - \bar{v}_i)^3 / \sum_j w_{ij}}{s_i^3} \tag{2}$$

Kish effective sample size:

$$n_{\text{eff},i} = \frac{\left(\sum_j w_{ij}\right)^2}{\sum_j w_{ij}^2} \tag{3}$$

Local coefficient of variation (a scale-free companion reading, derivable from equations 1–2):

$$CV_i = s_i / \bar{v}_i \tag{4}$$
Implementation note. The engine (core/stats_engines.py::calculate_gw_summary_stats) reuses the exact kernel-weight formulas already implemented for calculate_gwr (Fixed Gaussian, Fixed Bisquare, Adaptive Bisquare), so a bandwidth value has an identical meaning here as in GWR/MGWR. No new kernel logic was introduced, minimizing the correctness surface added by this tool.
3. Parameters

5. Interpretation Guide
Bandwidth trade-off. Too small a bandwidth produces noisy, erratic local statistics with low gw_neff everywhere; too large approaches the plain global mean/std and erases the spatial variation the tool exists to reveal. Map gw_std to check the constant-variance assumption behind global regression tools — sharp spatial variation in gw_std suggests a single global model will fit some areas much worse than others, and a GWR/MGWR model (or Spatial Regime Regression, if the variation aligns with a categorical boundary) may be worth trying instead.

Reading gw_skew alongside a modeling choice. A field whose gw_skew is strongly positive in some areas and near-zero in others is not well described by a single global skewness figure, and models that assume a symmetric error distribution (OLS, and Gaussian-family GLR) may fit poorly in the high-skew areas specifically. If gw_skew is persistently high across most of the study area for the dependent variable of a planned regression, consider Quantile Regression or the Poisson/Logistic GLR families over plain OLS.

See also: GWR · MGWR · Data Readiness Audit · Quantile Regression

06

Machine Learning and Explainable AI

Modern supervised-learning models (tree ensembles, gradient boosting across four engines, support vector machines, a small neural network, and a 2025-generation tabular foundation model) for predicting a continuous or categorical planning outcome, paired with the diagnostic scaffolding a spatial dataset specifically needs: a spatially blocked cross-validator (with a choice of two fold-assignment methods), a leaderboard for comparing model families on equal footing, and explainability that goes well beyond a single global importance ranking — SHAP contributions written back onto the map as symbolizable columns (Spatial Attribution Map), an exact, non-sampled per-field breakdown from a glass-box additive model (Explainable Boosting Machine), an action-oriented "what would have to change" view for a single record (DiCE Counterfactual Explanation), and distribution-free prediction intervals with a proven coverage guarantee for any regression model in the group (Conformal Prediction Interval). Every tool here builds on the same optional scikit-learn dependency already used elsewhere in the plugin (Similarity Search, Multivariate Clustering); XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, shap, interpret, mapie, dice-ml, and tabpfn are additional optional packages installed the same way.

Always cross-validate before trusting an ML score. Every fitting tool in this group reports an in-sample fit metric (R2, accuracy) that overstates real-world performance, sometimes substantially for boosting and neural-network models. Run Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator and report that score, not the fitting tool's own in-sample number, whenever the result will inform an actual planning decision.
🌲

Random Forest Regression

random_forest_regression
An ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap resample of the records and a random subset of fields at every split, whose predictions are averaged — capturing non-linear relationships and field interactions with no distributional assumption, at the cost of interpretable coefficients.
1. Theoretical Background

Bagging plus feature randomness. Breiman (2001) combined two variance-reduction ideas into Random Forests: bagging (Breiman, 1996) — training each tree on an independent bootstrap resample and averaging — and random feature subsetting at every split, which decorrelates the trees further than bagging alone (highly correlated trees would just reproduce a single tree's error pattern when averaged). The combination is what makes the ensemble's variance drop faster than its bias rises as more trees are added, the mechanism behind Random Forest's practical robustness to overfitting relative to a single deep tree.

Out-of-bag error as a free internal check. Because each tree only sees ~63% of records in its bootstrap sample (the classic bagging fraction, \(1 - e^{-1}\)), the remaining ~37% ("out-of-bag") can be used to test that tree without a separate holdout split. Averaging each record's prediction across only the trees that did not see it produces the OOB score — an internal cross-validation estimate that costs nothing extra to compute, and the number this tool's report emphasizes over the more optimistic in-sample R2.

A structural limitation: no extrapolation. Because a tree's prediction is always the mean of training-record target values inside a leaf, Random Forest cannot extrapolate beyond the range of values it saw during training the way a linear model can — a field value 50% higher than anything in the training data still produces a prediction bounded by the training targets' observed range. This matters specifically for spatial prediction: applying a model fit on one district to a different district with a systematically different explanatory-field range (a much denser city core, for instance) risks silently flattened, underestimated predictions at the extremes, not a visible error. Checking whether the prediction layer's target field range matches the training layer's is a cheap, worthwhile sanity check before trusting predictions in an unseen area.

Why de-correlating trees actually reduces error: strength versus correlation. Breiman's (2001) original paper derives an upper bound on the forest's generalization error in terms of two competing quantities: the average individual tree's predictive strength, and the average correlation between trees' errors. Random feature subsetting at each split (governed indirectly by how many fields are available and how many candidate fields a split may consider) trades a small amount of per-tree strength for a larger reduction in inter-tree correlation — and because the error bound scales with correlation directly but only inversely with strength, this trade is usually a net win. This is the theoretical justification behind the practical advice to try more trees before tuning tree depth: adding trees at a fixed correlation/strength ratio (eq. 4 below) strictly cannot hurt the ensemble, while changing depth or the feature-subsetting rate changes that ratio and can help or hurt depending on the dataset.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Ensemble prediction (B trees, bootstrap sample \(\mathcal{D}_b\)):

$$\hat{f}(x) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x;\, \mathcal{D}_b) \tag{1}$$

Out-of-bag prediction (only trees where \(i \notin \mathcal{D}_b\)):

$$\hat{f}_{\text{OOB}}(x_i) = \frac{1}{|\{b: i \notin \mathcal{D}_b\}|}\sum_{b:\, i \notin \mathcal{D}_b} T_b(x_i) \tag{2}$$

Mean decrease in impurity feature importance (summed over all splits on field \(k\), all trees):

$$\text{Imp}(k) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{\text{splits on } k \text{ in } T_b} \Delta \text{impurity} \tag{3}$$

Breiman's (2001) generalization-error upper bound (\(\bar{\rho}\) = mean pairwise correlation between tree residuals, \(s\) = mean tree strength; the ratio this bound scales with is the theoretical basis for the strength/correlation trade-off above):

$$\text{PE}^{*} \le \bar{\rho}\,\frac{1-s^2}{s^2} \tag{4}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor with bootstrap=True, oob_score=True, n_jobs=-1 (core/ml_engines.py::fit_random_forest_regressor). Complete-case extraction and metric computation are shared with every other regression tool in this group via extract_regression_matrix/regression_metrics, so behavior around missing values is identical across the whole group. The reported feature_importances_ are Mean Decrease in Impurity (eq. 3) — biased toward high-cardinality continuous fields relative to low-cardinality ones (Strobl et al., 2007); Permutation Feature Importance gives an unbiased alternative ranking on the same fitted model.

5. Interpretation Guide
OOB score over in-sample R2. A large gap between OOB score and in-sample R2 signals overfitting — reduce Max tree depth or raise Minimum samples per leaf. Feature importances rank predictive contribution, not causal effect direction or magnitude; pair with SHAP Spatial Attribution Map for direction and geographic location of effect, and Model Residual Spatial Autocorrelation Check to confirm no spatial structure was left unexplained.

Predicting onto areas outside the training range. If Random Forest Regression will be used to predict onto parcels or districts the training data did not cover, check that the explanatory fields' ranges in the prediction area overlap the training area's ranges (Data Readiness Audit reports field ranges for exactly this purpose). Predictions for out-of-range inputs are not flagged automatically — they are simply clamped toward the nearest training leaf's average, which can look plausible while being systematically wrong.

A practical tuning order, grounded in the strength/correlation trade-off. Per equation 4, raise Number of trees first — it is the one setting that cannot make the ensemble worse, only more stable, and is worth generously over-provisioning before touching anything else (200 is a reasonable default; there is rarely harm in 500–1000 for a one-off analysis where a few extra seconds of runtime is a non-issue). Only after that, treat Max tree depth and Minimum samples per leaf as the actual regularization knobs: both directly reduce individual tree strength, so tightening them helps when OOB score and in-sample R2 diverge sharply (overfitting), but can hurt if pushed too far on a dataset that genuinely needs deep splits to capture real non-linear structure.

See also: Extra Trees Regression · SHAP Spatial Attribution Map · Spatial k-Fold CV Evaluator · Generalized Linear Regression

Strobl, C., Boulesteix, A.-L., Zeileis, A. & Hothorn, T. (2007). "Bias in Random Forest Variable Importance Measures: Illustrations, Sources and a Solution." BMC Bioinformatics 8: 25. DOI: 10.1186/1471-2105-8-25 — Documents the Mean Decrease in Impurity bias noted above.

🌲

Random Forest Classification

random_forest_classification
The classification counterpart of Random Forest Regression: an ensemble of bootstrap-trained trees voting by averaged class probability, for predicting a categorical outcome (land-use class, zoning category) instead of a continuous one.
1. Theoretical Background

Breiman's (2001) same bagging-plus-feature-randomness construction applies directly to classification: each tree votes a class probability distribution (the fraction of training records of each class in the leaf a query point falls into), and the forest averages those distributions across trees. As in the regression case, this reduces variance far more effectively than a single tree while requiring no distributional assumptions about the class boundary shape — Random Forest can fit boundaries no linear or simple parametric classifier could represent.

Class imbalance is the main practical hazard. A forest optimizing overall accuracy on an imbalanced target (a rare zoning category, an uncommon land-use class) can reach a high accuracy score simply by defaulting toward the majority class on ambiguous records — the well-known "accuracy paradox." This is why the report emphasizes per-class precision/recall/F1 and the full confusion matrix over the single accuracy number: a model that never predicts the minority class can still show high headline accuracy while being useless for the planning question that motivated collecting that class in the first place.

Vote fractions are not automatically calibrated probabilities. rf_conf is the fraction of trees voting for the predicted class — a genuine confidence signal, but Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (2005) showed tree-ensemble vote fractions are not, in general, well-calibrated probabilities: a set of records with rf_conf near 0.7 will not necessarily turn out to be correct roughly 70% of the time. Treat rf_conf as a reliable ranking of relative confidence across records (useful for prioritizing which predictions to field-verify first) rather than as a literal probability to plug into a downstream risk calculation without separate calibration.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Per-tree leaf class probability (leaf \(\ell\), class \(c\), training counts \(n_{\ell c}\)):

$$\hat{P}_b(y=c \mid x) = \frac{n_{\ell(x) c}}{\sum_{c'} n_{\ell(x) c'}} \tag{1}$$

Forest-averaged class probability and prediction:

$$\hat{P}(y=c \mid x) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat{P}_b(y=c \mid x), \qquad \hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_c \hat{P}(y=c \mid x) \tag{2}$$

Macro-averaged F1, the single-number summary this tool's report favors over raw accuracy on imbalanced targets (\(K\) classes, per-class \(F1_c\)):

$$\text{Macro-}F1 = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{c=1}^{K} F1_c, \qquad F1_c = \frac{2\,\text{Precision}_c\cdot\text{Recall}_c}{\text{Precision}_c + \text{Recall}_c} \tag{3}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier with the same bootstrap=True, oob_score=True configuration as the regression tool (core/ml_engines.py::fit_random_forest_classifier). Class labels are the sorted set of distinct values seen in the target field among complete records — reviewed in the report before the confusion matrix, since a class with only a handful of examples will be predicted unreliably regardless of forest size.
3. Parameters

FieldTypeDescription

5. Interpretation Guide
Look past accuracy. Check per-class recall for the classes that actually matter for your planning question before trusting a headline accuracy figure, especially with an imbalanced class distribution. Treat rf_conf as a mappable confidence surface: low-confidence areas are where field verification or additional explanatory data would improve the model most.

When rf_conf needs to be a real probability, not just a ranking. If a downstream calculation actually needs calibrated probabilities (for example, combining rf_conf with a cost figure to estimate expected loss), fit a separate calibration step outside this plugin (Platt scaling or isotonic regression against a held-out set) rather than using rf_conf directly — this tool reports the ensemble's raw vote fraction, deliberately, so its meaning stays simple and consistent across every classification tool in this group.

Reading macro-F1 versus accuracy in the report. Because macro-F1 (eq. 3) averages each class's F1 with equal weight regardless of how many records it has, a rare class dragging macro-F1 down while overall accuracy stays high is a direct, quantified signal of exactly the accuracy-paradox risk described above — a large gap between accuracy and macro-F1 is the single fastest sanity check for whether a headline accuracy figure is safe to report on its own.

See also: Extra Trees Classification · SHAP Global Feature Importance · Spatial k-Fold CV Evaluator

Extra Trees Regression

extra_trees_regression
Extremely randomized trees (Geurts, Ernst & Wehenkel, 2006): like Random Forest, an ensemble of trees averaged together, but each tree also picks its split threshold at random instead of searching for the locally optimal one — trading a little per-tree accuracy for lower ensemble variance and faster training.
1. Theoretical Background

Random Forest already randomizes which fields are considered at each split; Extra Trees goes one step further and randomizes the split threshold itself for each considered field, picking one uniformly at random rather than the value that best separates the training data at that node. Geurts, Ernst and Wehenkel (2006) show this additional randomization reduces variance more than it increases bias for many datasets, and — because no per-split optimal-threshold search is performed — training is also meaningfully faster. Extra Trees also does not bootstrap-resample by default (each tree sees the full dataset), so this tool reports no out-of-bag score; use Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator for an honest out-of-sample estimate instead.

A cross-check, not a replacement. Because Random Forest and Extra Trees differ only in their source of randomness, running both on the same fields and comparing feature-importance rankings and R2 is a useful robustness check: close agreement is reassuring evidence the pattern is real rather than an artifact of one algorithm's particular randomization scheme.

When the randomized-threshold trade favors Extra Trees. Geurts, Ernst and Wehenkel (2006) found the variance-reduction benefit of random thresholds is most pronounced with noisy fields and a modest number of training records — exactly the profile of many single-district or single-city planning datasets, where a handful of explanatory fields may carry measurement noise (a manually digitized road-density figure, a survey-derived score). On very clean, large datasets the two ensembles tend to converge to similar accuracy, and Random Forest's optimal-threshold search may edge ahead slightly; the two-tool comparison this section recommends is the practical way to find out which regime a given dataset falls into rather than assuming one in advance.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Split-threshold selection (field \(k\), value range \([a,b]\) at the current node — the sole mechanical difference from Random Forest's optimal-threshold search):

$$\text{threshold} \sim \text{Uniform}(a, b) \tag{1}$$

Ensemble prediction and feature importance otherwise follow the same averaging formulas as Random Forest Regression (equations 1 and 3 there); the same strength/correlation generalization-error bound (Random Forest Regression, eq. 4) also governs Extra Trees, with the randomized-threshold mechanism pushing further along the correlation axis than Random Forest's feature-subsetting alone.

Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.ensemble.ExtraTreesRegressor with bootstrap=True enabled (so an OOB score is still available in this plugin's configuration) via core/ml_engines.py::fit_extra_trees_regressor, sharing the same complete-case extraction and metrics helpers as every other regression tool in this group.

5. Interpretation Guide
Use as a cross-check against Random Forest Regression rather than in isolation; agreement between the two increases confidence in the explanatory-field ranking. No OOB score is reported — always confirm with Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator before reporting an R2 figure.

The same no-extrapolation limitation applies here. Extra Trees averages leaf-level training targets exactly as Random Forest does, so the extrapolation caveat in Random Forest Regression's interpretation guide (predictions for out-of-range explanatory-field values are clamped, not flagged) applies identically — check the prediction area's field ranges against the training layer's before trusting predictions in a substantially different subregion.

What a large Random Forest/Extra Trees gap suggests. Because the two engines differ in exactly one mechanical respect (optimized versus randomized split thresholds), a large R2 gap between them on the same fields is informative in a specific way: it suggests the outcome depends on split thresholds being placed precisely at the "right" values in the data rather than merely in the right neighborhood — often a sign of a genuinely sharp, threshold-like effect (a zoning cutoff, a distance band) rather than a smoothly varying relationship, worth investigating with a Partial Dependence Report on the suspected field.

Extra Trees Classification

extra_trees_classification
The classification counterpart of Extra Trees Regression: an ensemble voting by averaged class probability, with each tree's split threshold chosen at random rather than optimized — usually lower variance and faster training than Random Forest Classification, at a small per-tree accuracy cost.
1. Theoretical Background

Geurts, Ernst and Wehenkel's (2006) extremely-randomized-split construction applies identically to classification: each tree still votes a leaf-based class probability distribution, but the random split thresholds decorrelate the trees further than Random Forest's optimal-threshold search does, which can help on noisy planning data with many correlated explanatory fields.

As with the regression version, et_conf is a vote fraction, not an automatically calibrated probability — the same caveat noted for Random Forest Classification (Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana, 2005) applies here without modification.

Training-time savings compound across a full comparison workflow. Because Extra Trees skips the per-split optimal-threshold search entirely, it is typically the fastest tree-ensemble classifier to fit in this group — a modest advantage on a single run, but a meaningful one when running ML Model Comparison across several model families, or when repeatedly refitting during Permutation Feature Importance's many-repeat shuffling procedure on a large layer.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Follows the same leaf-probability averaging as Random Forest Classification (equations 1–2 there); the only mechanical difference is the random, rather than optimized, split-threshold search at each node (equation 1 of Extra Trees Regression). Macro-F1 (Random Forest Classification, eq. 3) is reported identically here.

Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.ensemble.ExtraTreesClassifier with bootstrap=True via core/ml_engines.py::fit_extra_trees_classifier, sharing the same classification-metrics helper (accuracy, confusion matrix, per-class precision/recall/F1) as every other classification tool in this group.

Reading disagreement between the two ensembles. When Random Forest and Extra Trees disagree on a specific record's predicted class, that record sits near a genuinely ambiguous region of the decision boundary rather than one algorithm simply being "wrong" — such records are good candidates for field verification or for review with SHAP Local Explanation Report to see which fields each model weighted differently.

Building an ensemble-of-ensembles view. For a genuinely important classification decision, it is reasonable to run Random Forest, Extra Trees, and at least one Gradient Boosting engine on the same fields and treat a record's classification as more trustworthy the more of these independently-randomized models agree on it — an informal but practical extension of the same variance-reduction logic that makes any single one of these ensembles work, applied one level up across model families rather than across trees within one family.

Support Vector Regression (SVR)

support_vector_regression
Finds a function that stays within an epsilon-wide tolerance tube around as many training points as possible, using only the points outside that tube (the support vectors) to shape the fit — capable of smooth non-linear relationships (RBF kernel) or a robust linear fit (Linear kernel), with no feature importances of its own.
1. Theoretical Background

From maximum-margin classification to regression. Cortes and Vapnik (1995) introduced the maximum-margin idea behind support vector machines for classification; Vapnik's (1995, 1998) \(\varepsilon\)-insensitive loss extended it to regression: any prediction error smaller than \(\varepsilon\) is not penalized at all, so the fitted function only needs to stay within a tolerance tube of the data, and only the points that violate that tube (the support vectors) influence the final function. This produces a sparse solution — most training points contribute nothing to the fit — and, with a non-linear kernel, an implicit mapping to a higher-dimensional feature space (the "kernel trick") without ever computing that mapping explicitly.

No native feature importance. Unlike a tree ensemble, SVR's fitted function has no natural decomposition into per-field contributions, especially with a non-linear kernel where the decision surface lives in an implicit transformed space. This tool answers "how well can this be predicted," not "which field matters most" — pair it with a tree-based tool or Permutation Feature Importance (which works for any model, including this one) when the explanatory question matters as much as predictive accuracy.

A training-cost ceiling on large layers. Solving the SVR quadratic program scales roughly quadratically to cubically with the number of training records, unlike a tree ensemble's near-linear scaling — the practical reason SVR is offered here as one option among several rather than a default. On typical single-district or single-city planning layers (hundreds to a few thousand parcels) this is rarely noticeable; on a province-scale layer with tens of thousands of records, expect training time to grow far faster than the record count, and a tree-based or gradient-boosting engine will usually be the more practical choice regardless of accuracy.

2. Mathematical Formulation

\(\varepsilon\)-insensitive loss:

$$L_\varepsilon(y, \hat{y}) = \max(0,\, |y - \hat{y}| - \varepsilon) \tag{1}$$

Primal objective (kernel feature map \(\phi\)):

$$\min_{w,b} \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert w \rVert^2 + C\sum_i L_\varepsilon(y_i,\, w'\phi(x_i)+b) \tag{2}$$

RBF kernel (this tool's default):

$$K(x_i, x_j) = \exp\!\left(-\gamma \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2\right) \tag{3}$$

Dual formulation actually solved (Lagrange multipliers \(\alpha_i, \alpha_i^{*}\); only points with non-zero \(\alpha\) — the support vectors — appear in the final sum):

$$\hat{y}(x) = \sum_{i} (\alpha_i - \alpha_i^{*})\, K(x_i, x) + b \tag{4}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.svm.SVR inside a StandardScaler pipeline (core/ml_engines.py::fit_svr) — both features and the target are standardized internally before fitting, since SVR is scale-sensitive, and predictions are converted back to the original target scale automatically.
3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
TARGETNumeric Field——Target field
FEATURESNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldExplanatory fields
KERNELEnumRBFLinear / RBF / PolynomialKernel function
CDouble1.00.001–1000Regularization strength
EPSILONDouble0.10.0–10.0Tolerance tube width
OUTPUTVector Layer——Output predictions layer
4. Output Description
FieldTypeDescription
svr_predDoublePredicted value (converted back from the standardized fit)
svr_residDoubleObserved minus predicted
svr_usedInteger1 if used to fit and predict, 0 otherwise
5. Interpretation Guide
Epsilon and C together control smoothness. A larger epsilon ignores small residuals and produces a simpler, flatter fit; a smaller epsilon fits more closely but risks overfitting noise. Raise C to fit training data more tightly, lower it for a smoother, more regularized fit. Use Random Forest Regression alongside this tool to get feature importances SVR cannot provide.

Choosing a kernel. Start with Linear when there is reason to expect an approximately monotonic, additive relationship — it is far faster to fit and its coefficients, while not exposed as feature_importances_, at least correspond to a fixed direction of effect per field. Move to RBF specifically when Linear's R2 (or a residual plot) suggests curvature the linear kernel cannot capture; Polynomial is rarely the best choice on planning-scale data and is included mainly for completeness and comparison.

What a small support-vector count means. Because only points that violate the epsilon tube become support vectors (eq. 4), a fit where nearly every record ends up as a support vector suggests epsilon is too small for this data's noise level — the model is straining to touch almost every point rather than finding a genuinely simpler underlying tube. Conversely, very few support vectors alongside poor R2 suggests epsilon is too large, discarding real signal as within-tolerance noise. This plugin does not currently surface the support-vector count directly, but it is a concept worth understanding when C and Epsilon tuning produces a fit that neither over- nor under-fits convincingly.

See also: Support Vector Classification · Random Forest Regression · Permutation Feature Importance

Support Vector Classification (SVC)

support_vector_classification
Finds the maximum-margin decision boundary (linear, or non-linear via the RBF/Polynomial kernel trick) separating classes, defined only by the closest boundary points (the support vectors) — strong for cleanly or non-linearly separable classes, with no native feature importances.
1. Theoretical Background

Cortes and Vapnik's (1995) original formulation is a classifier: among all hyperplanes that separate two classes, choose the one maximizing the margin (distance) to the nearest points of either class — a choice that provably minimizes an upper bound on generalization error, not just training error. With the kernel trick, the same margin-maximization logic operates in an implicit, higher-dimensional feature space, letting SVC fit curved boundaries no linear separator could represent. Class probabilities (used here for the confidence field) are estimated via an internal cross-validated calibration step (Platt scaling), which is why fitting an SVC is somewhat more expensive than an equivalently sized Random Forest.

Beyond two classes. The margin-maximization objective (eq. 1) is inherently a two-class construction; scikit-learn extends it to more than two classes via a one-vs-one scheme, training a separate binary SVC for every pair of classes and combining their votes. With many classes this means fitting \(\binom{k}{2}\) models internally — invisible to the user, but part of why multi-class SVC on a target field with many categories can be noticeably slower to fit than the equivalent Random Forest Classification, which handles any number of classes with a single tree-growing pass.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Margin-maximization primal (soft-margin, kernel feature map \(\phi\)):

$$\min_{w,b,\xi} \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert w \rVert^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i \quad \text{s.t.}\quad y_i(w'\phi(x_i)+b) \ge 1-\xi_i,\ \xi_i \ge 0 \tag{1}$$

Decision function:

$$\hat{y}(x) = \text{sign}\!\left(\sum_{i \in \text{SV}} \alpha_i y_i K(x_i, x) + b\right) \tag{2}$$

Platt scaling — the calibration model layered on top of the raw decision function \(f(x)\) to produce svc_conf (\(A, B\) fit by maximum likelihood against the training labels):

$$P(y=1 \mid f(x)) = \frac{1}{1+\exp(A\,f(x)+B)} \tag{3}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.svm.SVC(probability=True) inside a StandardScaler pipeline (core/ml_engines.py::fit_svc) — features are standardized internally, no manual scaling needed.
3. Parameters

5. Interpretation Guide
Use RBF/Polynomial when classes are not linearly separable, Linear when they roughly are and speed matters. Raise C to fit the training boundary more tightly (risking overfitting near-ambiguous cases), lower it for a wider-margin, more regularized boundary. Pair with Random Forest Classification for feature importances SVC cannot provide.

svc_conf reflects Platt-scaled calibration, not the raw margin. Because the confidence field comes from a separate calibration model fit on top of the SVC decision function rather than the margin distance itself, it is somewhat more trustworthy as an actual probability than a raw ensemble vote fraction (Random Forest's rf_conf) — but it is still fit on the same training data being classified, so the same general caution about validating on held-out data (Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator) applies before using svc_conf in a downstream calculation.

Watch fit time on target fields with many categories. Because the one-vs-one extension fits \(\binom{k}{2}\) internal binary models, a target field with, say, 8 zoning categories fits 28 internal SVCs rather than 1 — still usually fast on planning-scale data, but worth knowing about before assuming SVC will scale the same way as Random Forest Classification does when a categorical field with many distinct values is used as the target.

See also: Support Vector Regression · Random Forest Classification

Gradient Boosting Regression (scikit-learn)

gbm_regression_sklearn
Gradient Boosting via scikit-learn's histogram-binned HistGradientBoostingRegressor: trees added sequentially, each fit to the residual error of the ensemble so far. Requires no extra package beyond scikit-learn (already used elsewhere in this plugin) — the zero-extra-install way to try boosting.
1. Theoretical Background

Boosting versus bagging. Where Random Forest and Extra Trees average many independently-trained trees (bagging), Friedman's (2001) Gradient Boosting Machine builds trees sequentially, each one fit specifically to the current ensemble's residual error via functional gradient descent in prediction space. This typically achieves lower bias than bagging at a given tree count — each new tree directly targets what the ensemble still gets wrong — but at higher variance and overfitting risk, since the sequential fitting process can eventually start fitting noise in the training residuals if allowed to run too long without regularization (few boosting rounds, shallow trees, a low learning rate).

Histogram binning for speed. This engine specifically uses scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingRegressor (inspired by LightGBM's histogram approach), which discretizes continuous features into a fixed number of bins before searching for splits — dramatically reducing split-search cost relative to the classical exact-greedy method, at the price of not exposing a native feature_importances_ array the way the tree-ensemble bagging tools in this group do.

Why this group offers four boosting engines rather than one. scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost all implement the same underlying idea (Friedman's sequential residual-fitting) but differ in split-search strategy, regularization, and tree-growth shape — differences that can matter on a specific dataset in ways that are hard to predict in advance. This engine's specific role is the "no extra install, reasonable default" option: it is the only one of the four that adds no new optional package beyond scikit-learn (already required for most of this group), making it the natural first boosting engine to try before installing XGBoost, LightGBM, or CatBoost specifically to compare.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Additive ensemble after M boosting rounds:

$$F_M(x) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \nu \cdot h_m(x) \tag{1}$$

Each round fits a tree to the negative gradient of the loss (squared error shown; \(\nu\)=learning rate):

$$h_m = \arg\min_h \sum_i \left(-\left[\frac{\partial L(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i))}{\partial F_{m-1}(x_i)}\right] - h(x_i)\right)^2 \tag{2}$$

Learning-rate/round-count trade-off: shrinking \(\nu\) while raising \(M\) proportionally traces out approximately the same final fit (Friedman, 2001) but with a smoother, less overfitting-prone optimization path — the formal justification behind the "lower the rate and raise the round count together" advice below:

$$F_M(x) \approx F_{M'}(x) \text{ when } \nu \cdot M \approx \nu' \cdot M' \tag{3}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gbm_regressor, engine="sklearn"). Because this engine exposes no native feature importances, the report explicitly directs the analyst to Permutation Feature Importance instead of showing an empty or misleading table.

5. Interpretation Guide
Treat in-sample R2 as an upper bound. Boosting fits training data more closely than bagging at a given tree count, so the gap between in-sample and cross-validated R2 is typically larger here than for Random Forest. Always confirm with Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator. A high learning rate combined with many boosting rounds is the most common cause of severe overfitting — lower the rate and raise the round count together for a more conservative fit.

Using this engine as the baseline in a four-engine comparison. Because it needs no extra install, run this engine first and treat its cross-validated score as the baseline to beat before installing XGBoost, LightGBM, or CatBoost — if all four engines land within a small margin of each other (typical on many planning datasets), the extra packages add engineering overhead without a meaningful accuracy gain, and this engine alone may be sufficient going forward.

See also: Gradient Boosting Regression (XGBoost) · Gradient Boosting Regression (LightGBM) · Gradient Boosting Regression (CatBoost) · Random Forest Regression · Spatial k-Fold CV Evaluator
6. Literature

Friedman, J.H. (2001). "Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine." Annals of Statistics 29(5): 1189–1232. DOI: 10.1214/aos/1013203451 — The original Gradient Boosting paper; source of the learning-rate/round-count trade-off (eq. 3).

Friedman, J.H. (2002). "Stochastic Gradient Boosting." Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 38(4): 367–378. DOI: 10.1016/S0167-9473(01)00065-2 — Introduces row subsampling per boosting round as a further variance-reduction technique, used internally by several of this group's engines.

Gradient Boosting Regression (XGBoost)optional

gbm_regression_xgboost
Gradient Boosting via XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016): second-order (Newton) boosting with built-in L1/L2 regularization. Requires the optional xgboost package.
1. Theoretical Background

Chen and Guestrin (2016) reformulated Friedman's gradient boosting using a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss (not just the first-order gradient), giving each tree a more precise target and enabling a closed-form optimal leaf-weight formula. XGBoost adds explicit L1/L2 penalties directly into the split-gain criterion, which tends to make it somewhat more resistant to overfitting than a plain first-order implementation at equivalent settings — one reason it became the dominant gradient boosting library in machine-learning competitions in the years following its release.

Second-order information sharpens each tree's target. A first-order method (like the plain functional gradient descent in Friedman's original formulation) knows only the slope of the loss at the current prediction; XGBoost's use of the Hessian \(h_i\) (eq. 1) additionally captures the loss's curvature, letting the optimal leaf weight (the closed-form minimizer of eq. 1 for a fixed tree structure) be computed directly rather than approximated — in practice this tends to produce a more precisely targeted correction per round, particularly useful when residuals are heteroscedastic (uneven in spread) across the study area.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Regularized objective at round \(m\) (\(g_i, h_i\) = first/second-order loss gradients; \(\Omega\) = tree complexity penalty):

$$\mathcal{L}^{(m)} = \sum_i \left[g_i h_m(x_i) + \tfrac{1}{2}h_i h_m(x_i)^2\right] + \Omega(h_m) \tag{1}$$

Complexity penalty (leaf count \(T\), leaf weights \(w_j\)):

$$\Omega(h) = \gamma T + \tfrac{1}{2}\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2 \tag{2}$$

Closed-form optimal weight for leaf \(j\) given a fixed tree structure (\(I_j\) = records falling in leaf \(j\)) — the direct payoff of using second-order information:

$$w_j^{*} = -\frac{\sum_{i \in I_j} g_i}{\sum_{i \in I_j} h_i + \lambda} \tag{3}$$
Implementation note. Wraps xgboost.XGBRegressor (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gbm_regressor, engine="xgboost"), exposing native gain-based feature importances.

5. Interpretation Guide
XGBoost's built-in regularization makes it somewhat more overfitting-resistant than the scikit-learn engine at default settings, but always confirm with Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator. Compare against the scikit-learn and LightGBM engines on the same fields; strong cross-engine agreement is reassuring evidence the fit is real rather than engine-specific.

Gain-based importances versus MDI. This engine's native feature importances are gain-based (the average split-gain improvement attributed to each field), a conceptually different quantity from Random Forest's Mean Decrease in Impurity, though both are commonly read the same way. The two rankings usually agree on the top fields for a well-behaved planning dataset; a sharp disagreement between them is a signal to check Permutation Feature Importance as an unbiased tie-breaker rather than trusting either ranking alone.

Gradient Boosting Regression (LightGBM)optional

gbm_regression_lightgbm
Gradient Boosting via LightGBM (Ke et al., 2017): trees grown leaf-wise (expanding whichever leaf reduces error most) instead of level-wise — usually faster and able to fit sharper local patterns on larger datasets. Requires the optional lightgbm package.
1. Theoretical Background

Most tree-growth algorithms (including the scikit-learn and XGBoost engines above, by default) grow level-wise — expanding every leaf at the current depth before going deeper. Ke et al. (2017) instead grow LightGBM's trees leaf-wise: at each step, split whichever single leaf across the whole tree reduces loss the most, regardless of depth. For a fixed number of leaves this typically reaches lower loss than level-wise growth, but it can also produce deeper, more overfitting-prone trees on small datasets if left unconstrained — the reason this tool exposes Max tree depth as a direct guard rail.

Two further speed techniques, most useful on large layers. Ke et al. (2017) also introduced Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) — keeping all records with large gradients (the ones the ensemble is still fitting poorly) but only a random subsample of small-gradient records for computing each split, since well-fit records contribute little new information — and Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB), which merges mutually-exclusive sparse fields into a single bundle to reduce the effective feature count during split search. Both techniques matter most on large, high-dimensional tables; on a typical single-district planning layer with a modest field count, LightGBM's practical speed edge over the other engines is usually small, and the leaf-wise growth strategy above is the more consequential difference.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Follows the same additive-ensemble and gradient-fitting formulation as Gradient Boosting Regression (scikit-learn), equations 1–2 there; the mechanical difference is leaf-wise rather than level-wise tree growth, plus LightGBM's histogram-based split search and gradient-based one-side sampling for further speed on large datasets. GOSS's sampling probability for a small-gradient record is not uniform but weighted to keep the gradient-sum estimate unbiased: retained small-gradient records are up-weighted by a constant factor \((1-a)/b\) (top fraction \(a\) kept in full, remaining fraction sampled at rate \(b\)) when accumulating split-gain statistics, exactly compensating for the records that were dropped.

Implementation note. Wraps lightgbm.LGBMRegressor (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gbm_regressor, engine="lightgbm"), exposing native feature importances.
