5. Interpretation Guide
The most overfitting-prone engine on small datasets. Leaf-wise growth fits training data very closely — reduce Max tree depth or lower the learning rate if in-sample R2 looks suspiciously close to 1.0, and always confirm with Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator. LightGBM tends to pull ahead of the other two engines on larger datasets and roughly match them on small single-district planning datasets.

Max tree depth matters more here than for level-wise engines. Because leaf-wise growth can produce a small number of very deep, narrow branches rather than a broad, shallow tree, Max tree depth is a more load-bearing regularization knob for LightGBM than it is for the scikit-learn or XGBoost engines — when comparing all engines side by side at their default settings, remember that LightGBM's default depth guard is doing more work than the others' to keep the fit conservative.

Gradient Boosting Classification (scikit-learn)

gbm_classification_sklearn
The classification counterpart of Gradient Boosting Regression (scikit-learn): trees added sequentially to correct the ensemble's classification errors, via scikit-learn's histogram-binned HistGradientBoostingClassifier. No extra package beyond scikit-learn required.
1. Theoretical Background

Friedman's (2001) gradient boosting framework applies to classification via a logistic (or multinomial) loss in place of squared error — each round's tree still fits the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current ensemble's predictions, now measured on the log-odds scale rather than the raw target scale. As with the regression engine, no native feature importances are exposed by scikit-learn's histogram-based implementation.

Why the log-odds scale matters for interpretation. Because each boosting round fits a residual on the log-odds scale rather than the probability scale, the ensemble's raw score before the final softmax/sigmoid conversion is not itself a probability and is not exposed by this tool — only the final gbm_conf (post-conversion) is. This is a purely mechanical detail of how gradient boosting classification works, but it explains why gbm_conf cannot be decomposed into a simple sum of per-round contributions the way a plain additive regression model's prediction can; SHAP is the tool in this group designed specifically to recover a per-field decomposition from a model like this one.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Follows the same additive-ensemble structure as Gradient Boosting Regression (equation 1 there), with the gradient of equation 2 computed against the binomial/multinomial deviance loss instead of squared error, and predictions converted to class probabilities via a softmax (or sigmoid, for two classes) of the ensemble's raw score. Binomial deviance for the two-class case, evaluated at the ensemble's raw score \(F(x_i)\):

$$L(y_i, F(x_i)) = \log\!\left(1+e^{-2y_iF(x_i)}\right), \qquad y_i \in \{-1,+1\} \tag{1}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gbm_classifier, engine="sklearn"). No native feature importances — the report directs the analyst to Permutation Feature Importance.

Gradient Boosting Classification (XGBoost)optional

gbm_classification_xgboost
The classification counterpart of Gradient Boosting Regression (XGBoost): second-order boosting with built-in L1/L2 regularization and native gain-based feature importances. Requires the optional xgboost package.
1. Theoretical Background

Chen and Guestrin's (2016) second-order boosting formulation (see Gradient Boosting Regression (XGBoost), equations 1–2) applies to classification via the binomial/multinomial deviance loss, with the same explicit L1/L2 leaf-weight regularization built into the split-gain criterion.

Where the second-order advantage shows up most. The Hessian-informed leaf weights that give XGBoost regression a more precisely targeted correction per round (see the regression entry) matter somewhat differently for classification: because the binomial deviance loss's curvature varies with how confident the current ensemble already is about a record (near-certain predictions have a flatter loss curvature than borderline ones), second-order information lets XGBoost allocate less correction effort to already-confident, easy records and more to borderline ones — a natural fit for planning classification tasks where most records are easy and a genuinely ambiguous minority drive most of the error.

Regularization interacts with class imbalance. The L1/L2 leaf-weight penalty (Gradient Boosting Regression (XGBoost), eq. 2) shrinks every leaf's contribution toward zero somewhat, which on an imbalanced target has an asymmetric practical effect: predictions for the minority class, already less confidently supported by fewer training examples, are pulled toward the majority-class default slightly more than majority-class predictions are — one contributor (alongside plain sample scarcity) to minority-class recall being the metric most worth watching closely for this engine specifically.

Implementation note. Wraps xgboost.XGBClassifier (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gbm_classifier, engine="xgboost").

Native importances here are gain-based, not vote fractions. Unlike Random Forest Classification's Mean Decrease in Impurity, XGBoost's default importances rank fields by average split-gain — conceptually similar but not numerically comparable across engines. When reporting a "top predictive fields" ranking, name which engine and importance type produced it rather than treating the ranking as engine-agnostic.

Gradient Boosting Classification (LightGBM)optional

gbm_classification_lightgbm
The classification counterpart of Gradient Boosting Regression (LightGBM): leaf-wise tree growth for speed and sharper local decision boundaries. Requires the optional lightgbm package.
1. Theoretical Background

Ke et al.'s (2017) leaf-wise growth strategy (see Gradient Boosting Regression (LightGBM)) applies unchanged to classification, fitting the binomial/multinomial deviance gradient at each round instead of squared error.

Sharper decision boundaries, at an overfitting cost. Because leaf-wise growth concentrates splitting effort wherever the loss is currently worst, LightGBM classification can carve out sharper, more localized decision boundaries around a small cluster of hard-to-classify records than a level-wise engine growing the same number of leaves — useful when a genuine minority subclass exists, but also the mechanism behind this engine's greater tendency to overfit small training sets if Max tree depth and learning rate are not actively constrained.

GOSS's small-gradient down-sampling has a class-imbalance interaction worth knowing. Because minority-class records typically carry larger gradients for longer during training (the ensemble takes more rounds to become confident about them), GOSS's keep-large-gradients rule (LightGBM Regression) tends to retain minority-class records preferentially relative to easy majority-class ones — a modest, incidental partial counterweight to the accuracy-paradox risk, though not a substitute for actively checking per-class recall.

Implementation note. Wraps lightgbm.LGBMClassifier (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gbm_classifier, engine="lightgbm").

Gradient Boosting Regression (CatBoost)optional

gbm_regression_catboost
Gradient Boosting via CatBoost (Prokhorenkova, Gusev, Vorobev, Dorogush & Gulin, NeurIPS 2018): ordered boosting to remove a subtle target-leakage bias present in classical gradient boosting, plus symmetric ("oblivious") trees. Requires the optional catboost package.
1. Theoretical Background

Ordered boosting and prediction shift. In classical gradient boosting (as used by the scikit-learn, XGBoost, and LightGBM engines above), the gradient used to fit tree \(m\) for training example \(i\) is computed from a model, \(F_{m-1}\), that was itself fit using example \(i\)'s own target value in earlier rounds. Prokhorenkova et al. (2018) showed this creates a systematic bias they call prediction shift: the in-sample gradient distribution the trees are fit to is subtly different from the gradient distribution a genuinely new point would produce, inflating in-sample fit quality by a small but real amount. CatBoost's fix, ordered boosting, computes each example's gradient using a model trained only on a random permutation of examples that precede it — effectively simulating out-of-sample gradients during training itself, at the cost of needing several such permutations internally to keep variance manageable.

Symmetric (oblivious) trees. Where scikit-learn, XGBoost, and LightGBM grow trees whose split choice can differ from node to node at the same depth, CatBoost's default trees are symmetric: every node at a given depth splits on the same feature and threshold. This is a stronger structural constraint — effectively a balanced decision table rather than an arbitrary binary tree — that evaluates faster and acts as an implicit regularizer, at some cost to how tightly any single tree can fit a locally idiosyncratic subregion of the feature space.

Categorical handling not exercised here. CatBoost's other headline feature — native categorical-field support via leakage-safe ordered target statistics, avoiding manual one-hot or target encoding — is not exercised by this plugin's pipeline, since every tool in this group takes numeric explanatory fields only. What this tool actually adds over the other three GBM engines is exclusively the ordered-boosting and symmetric-tree behavior above.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Additive ensemble after M boosting rounds (as in every GBM engine in this group):

$$F_M(x) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \nu \cdot h_m(x) \tag{1}$$

Ordered boosting's gradient for example \(i\) at round \(m\) uses a model \(F_{m-1}^{(\sigma_{

$$\text{grad}_i^{(m)} = -\left[\frac{\partial L\!\left(y_i,\, F_{m-1}^{(\sigma_{
Implementation note. Wraps catboost.CatBoostRegressor with verbose=False and allow_writing_files=False (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gbm_regressor, engine="catboost"), exposing native, PredictionValuesChange-based feature importances.

5. Interpretation Guide
CatBoost's overfitting profile differs from a max-depth story alone. Because symmetric trees are already a strong regularizer, CatBoost at default settings often needs less manual depth-limiting than XGBoost or LightGBM to reach a comparable fit; a first read should still confirm with Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator rather than trusting in-sample R2. Compare fitted values against the other three GBM engines on the same fields — the four engines agreeing closely is stronger evidence the underlying relationship is real than any single engine's fit statistics alone.

When ordered boosting's benefit is largest. Prediction shift is most consequential on smaller training sets, where a training example's own influence on the model that produces its gradient is proportionally larger — exactly the single-district, hundreds-to-low-thousands-of-records regime this plugin most often operates in. On very large datasets the effect of any one point on the overall fit shrinks, and CatBoost's advantage over the other three engines tends to narrow; this is one reason CatBoost is worth trying specifically (not just as a completeness check) on smaller planning layers.

Gradient Boosting Classification (CatBoost)optional

gbm_classification_catboost
The classification counterpart of Gradient Boosting Regression (CatBoost): the same ordered-boosting and symmetric-tree machinery, fitting the classification log-loss gradient at each round instead of squared error. Requires the optional catboost package.
1. Theoretical Background

Prokhorenkova et al.'s (2018) ordered-boosting mechanism (see Gradient Boosting Regression (CatBoost)) applies unchanged to classification: each example's gradient is estimated from a model trained only on examples preceding it under a random permutation, avoiding the prediction-shift bias that comes from computing a training example's own gradient with a model that has already seen its target. Symmetric trees again act as an implicit regularizer, splitting on the same feature and threshold across an entire depth level.

Ordered boosting matters more for classification log-loss than squared error. Prediction shift's distortion is a function of how much a model's fitted value at a training point differs, on average, from what an honest out-of-sample prediction there would be. For classification's log-loss gradient, that distortion tends to be most consequential exactly where the model is already fairly confident — precisely the well-separated majority of records in a typically imbalanced planning classification target (e.g. most parcels clearly not redeveloping) — since a small amount of self-referential bias in a confident prediction's gradient can compound over many boosting rounds. Ordered boosting's out-of-sample-simulated gradients reduce this compounding, one of several reasons CatBoost was benchmarked as unusually competitive specifically on datasets with imbalanced or noisy targets.

Implementation note. Wraps catboost.CatBoostClassifier with verbose=False and allow_writing_files=False (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gbm_classifier, engine="catboost").

🧠

Neural Network Regression (MLP)

mlp_regression
A small feed-forward neural network (Multi-Layer Perceptron): explanatory fields pass through one or more hidden layers of weighted, non-linearly activated units before producing a prediction, with weights learned by gradient descent (backpropagation). Needs substantially more complete records than the tree-based tools in this group to fit reliably.
1. Theoretical Background

Universal approximation, at a data-hunger cost. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (1986) popularized backpropagation — efficient gradient computation through a multi-layer network via the chain rule — as the practical training method for MLPs, and Hornik, Stinchcombe and White (1989) later proved that a single hidden layer with enough units can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain arbitrarily well (the universal approximation theorem). In practice, however, an MLP needs far more complete training records than a comparably-sized tree ensemble to reach that approximation quality reliably, since gradient descent must estimate every connection weight from data rather than growing a discrete tree structure.

When it is worth the cost. On the modest single-district or single-city planning datasets typical of this plugin's use, Random Forest Regression or Gradient Boosting Regression usually match or beat an MLP with far easier interpretation and no convergence risk. Reach for this tool specifically when the sample is large and the relationship is expected to be smoothly, highly non-linear in a way tree splits approximate poorly (tree-based models produce axis-aligned step functions, not smooth curves).

Tabular data specifically favors tree ensembles. Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux (2022) documented, across a wide range of benchmark tabular datasets, that tree-based ensembles like Random Forest and Gradient Boosting continue to outperform neural networks including MLPs — attributing the gap to tabular data's typically irregular, non-smooth target functions and uninformative rotation-sensitive feature spaces, both of which favor axis-aligned tree splits over a smooth network function. This is not a criticism specific to this implementation; it is a documented, general property of the data type this entire plugin operates on, and the reason Random Forest/Gradient Boosting are positioned as the default choices throughout this group rather than this tool.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Layer-by-layer forward pass (activation \(\sigma\), typically ReLU in hidden layers):

$$h^{(l)} = \sigma\!\left(W^{(l)} h^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}\right), \qquad \hat{y} = W^{(L)} h^{(L-1)} + b^{(L)} \tag{1}$$

Weight update by stochastic gradient descent on squared error:

$$W^{(l)} \leftarrow W^{(l)} - \eta \frac{\partial}{\partial W^{(l)}}\left[\tfrac{1}{2}(y-\hat{y})^2\right] \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.neural_network.MLPRegressor inside a StandardScaler pipeline (core/ml_engines.py::fit_mlp_regressor) — features and target are standardized internally. The report shows training convergence status (iterations used versus the cap); a model that hits the cap without converging should not be trusted. Weight updates use scikit-learn's default Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015) rather than plain stochastic gradient descent — an adaptive per-parameter learning rate scheme that converges faster and more reliably than fixed-rate SGD on the kind of modest, noisy planning datasets this tool is used on, though "Maximum training iterations" still refers to Adam update steps, not a separate hyperparameter.

5. Interpretation Guide
A model that did not converge (see the report's convergence status) should not be trusted — raise Maximum iterations or simplify the hidden-layer sizes. Fewer, smaller layers reduce overfitting risk on modest planning datasets. This tool provides no feature importances; use Permutation Feature Importance for the only available ranking.

Justify reaching for this tool, don't default to it. Given the documented tabular-data disadvantage above, treat a decision to use MLP Regression over Random Forest/Gradient Boosting as one that needs its own justification (a specific, concrete reason to expect smooth non-linearity, plus a genuinely large sample) rather than trying every tool in the group and keeping whichever number looks best — Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator settles the comparison honestly if that justification is unclear.

See also: Neural Network Classification · Random Forest Regression · Permutation Feature Importance

Neural Network Classification (MLP)

mlp_classification
The classification counterpart of Neural Network Regression: explanatory fields pass through hidden layers before a softmax output layer assigns class probabilities, with weights learned by backpropagation.
1. Theoretical Background

The same universal-approximation and backpropagation foundations as Neural Network Regression apply here (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, 1986; Hornik, Stinchcombe & White, 1989), with a softmax output layer converting the final hidden layer's activations into a proper class-probability distribution and a cross-entropy loss in place of squared error.

The same tabular-data disadvantage documented for the regression version (Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux, 2022) applies to classification as well — on the modest, structured planning datasets this plugin targets, Random Forest Classification or a Gradient Boosting engine will usually match or beat an MLP classifier's accuracy with far less risk of a non-converging fit.

Why softmax, not one sigmoid per class. A separate independent sigmoid per class would let a record's class probabilities sum to something other than 1 (or nowhere near it); the softmax normalization (eq. 1) is specifically constructed so the outputs form a valid probability distribution over mutually exclusive classes, which is what a well-posed single-label classification problem requires and what the cross-entropy loss below is derived to optimize against.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Softmax output layer (\(z\) = final layer's pre-activation scores):

$$\hat{P}(y=c\mid x) = \frac{\exp(z_c)}{\sum_{c'}\exp(z_{c'})} \tag{1}$$

Cross-entropy loss the network minimizes during training (\(y_c\) = 1 if \(c\) is the true class, 0 otherwise):

$$L = -\sum_{c} y_c \log \hat{P}(y=c\mid x) \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.neural_network.MLPClassifier inside a StandardScaler pipeline (core/ml_engines.py::fit_mlp_classifier). Training convergence status is reported the same way as the regression tool.

5. Interpretation Guide
Prefer this tool only when sample size is large and class boundaries are expected to be smoothly non-linear; otherwise a tree-based classifier will usually match or beat it with far easier interpretation. Check the convergence status before trusting results.

mlp_conf and calibration. Like every classifier in this group, mlp_conf's softmax output is not automatically a calibrated probability despite being mathematically a valid probability distribution over classes; a network trained with too few records or too many iterations past convergence can produce overconfident, poorly calibrated softmax outputs. Treat mlp_conf as a relative ranking of confidence across records, and validate accuracy claims with Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator rather than the raw in-sample confidence values.

See also: Neural Network Regression · Random Forest Classification

Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator

spatial_kfold_cv_evaluator
Estimates honest out-of-sample accuracy for any model in this group using k-fold cross-validation with spatially contiguous folds (via K-Means on feature centroids) instead of randomly shuffled ones — removing the information leakage ordinary random CV allows under spatial autocorrelation.
1. Theoretical Background

Why random CV lies to you on spatial data. Standard k-fold cross-validation assumes training and held-out records are independent draws from the same distribution. Planning data almost never satisfies this: Tobler's (1970) first law of geography — "everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than far things" — means a randomly shuffled fold's test points are frequently right next to training points, letting the model implicitly "see" local information it should not have access to, and inflating the reported score. Roberts et al. (2017) formalize this concern across ecological and spatial modeling and recommend block-structured cross-validation specifically to remove it.

Spatial blocking via K-Means on coordinates. This tool's default fold method groups records into k spatially contiguous blocks by running K-Means clustering directly on feature centroid coordinates (not on the model's explanatory fields) — a simple, widely used way to approximate the spatial block-CV designs described in the environmental and ecological cross-validation literature without requiring the analyst to hand-draw block boundaries.

kNNDM: matching the CV design to the true prediction task, not just geographic compactness. K-Means blocking optimizes for tidy, compact folds, but says nothing about whether the resulting train/test distances actually resemble the distances a real deployment will face. Linnenbrink, Milà, Ludwig & Meyer (2024) introduced k-fold Nearest-Neighbour Distance Matching (kNNDM) to close that gap directly: rather than choosing folds for compactness, kNNDM searches among many candidate fold assignments for the one whose test-to-nearest-training-point distance distribution most closely matches the dataset's own leave-one-out nearest-neighbour distance distribution — the distances a genuinely new prediction location would actually face. A close match (small Wasserstein distance between the two distributions) indicates the cross-validation design itself is well-matched to the deployment scenario; K-Means blocking optimizes a different, purely geometric objective and can produce folds that look tidy on a map while still not matching this criterion well.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Fold assignment (K-Means spatial block) follows ordinary K-Means (see Multivariate Clustering) applied to centroid coordinates \((x_i, y_i)\) rather than attribute fields. For each fold \(f \in \{1,\dots,k\}\), the chosen model is refit on all records outside fold \(f\) and scored (R2 for regression, accuracy and macro-F1 for classification) on the held-out fold; the reported result is the mean and standard deviation of that score across all \(k\) folds.

kNNDM's selection criterion (\(G_j\) = leave-one-out nearest-neighbour distance distribution of the full dataset; \(G_{cv}\) = the candidate fold assignment's induced test-to-train nearest-neighbour distance distribution; \(W\) = 1-Wasserstein distance):

$$\text{fold assignment}^{*} = \arg\min_{\text{assignment}} \; W\!\left(G_j,\, G_{cv}(\text{assignment})\right) \tag{1}$$
Implementation note. Implemented in core/ml_engines.py::spatial_kfold_evaluate/spatial_kfold_assignment (K-Means block) and spatial_knndm_assignment (kNNDM). The kNNDM implementation is a practical Python port of the paper's kmeans-clustering variant — an overclustered partition is merged into k folds via many candidate KMeans groupings of different random seeds, keeping whichever candidate's \(G_{cv}\)/\(G_j\) mismatch is smallest, subject to a maximum-fold-size guard — not a byte-for-byte port of the CAST R package's exact search procedure. It costs more compute than K-Means blocking (many candidate fold assignments are evaluated) and can produce less visually tidy blocks on the map. The output layer's cv_fold field lets the analyst map the block layout directly regardless of which fold method was used; a fold with a markedly lower score than the others often corresponds to a spatially distinct subregion the model handles poorly, visible immediately once mapped.

5. Interpretation Guide
Report this score, not the fitting tool's in-sample score. A large standard deviation across folds means performance is uneven across the study area — check whether one region has systematically different data quality or a different underlying process. Choose Number of folds based on data size: 5 is a reasonable default, fewer (3) for smaller datasets, more (10) only with several hundred records or more.

Choosing a fold method. K-Means spatial block is faster and produces a fold layout that reads cleanly on a map — a reasonable default, and useful when the cv_fold breakdown itself is being interpreted as a simple regional split. Prefer kNNDM specifically when the honesty of the reported score matters more than a clean block map — for example, before reporting a cross-validated accuracy figure in a document that will inform a funding or zoning decision — since its fold assignment is chosen to match the actual out-of-sample prediction task rather than for geographic tidiness.

See also: ML Model Comparison · Random Forest Regression · Conformal Prediction Interval

Permutation Feature Importance

permutation_feature_importance
Ranks fields by how much a fitted model's score drops when that field is randomly shuffled (breaking its relationship with the target) while every other field stays intact — a model-agnostic importance measure that works for every model in this group, including SVM and MLP, neither of which expose a native importance ranking.
1. Theoretical Background

Breiman's (2001) Random Forest paper introduced permutation importance alongside mean-decrease-in-impurity importance as an alternative, model-internal measure computed from out-of-bag samples. Fisher, Rudin and Dominici (2019) later generalized the idea into a fully model-agnostic procedure — "Model Class Reliance" — applicable to any fitted predictor regardless of its internal structure, which is the version this tool implements: fit once on the full data, then repeatedly shuffle each field in turn and measure the resulting score drop, averaged over several repeats to control for the randomness the shuffling itself introduces.

Correlated fields split credit, they do not hide it. When two explanatory fields are strongly correlated, shuffling either one alone leaves the other largely able to substitute for the information lost — the model's score barely drops for either field individually, even though the pair jointly matters a great deal. This is a well-documented property of permutation importance (and of Mean Decrease in Impurity), not a bug in this implementation: a low importance score for two correlated fields considered separately does not mean the underlying concept they both measure is unimportant, only that no single one of them is uniquely necessary once the other is present. Checking a correlation matrix (Data Readiness Audit reports one) before interpreting a surprisingly low importance score is good practice.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Importance of field \(k\) (score \(s\) = R2 or accuracy; \(X_{\pi_k}\) = data with field \(k\) permuted):

$$\text{Imp}(k) = s(model, X, y) - \mathbb{E}_{\pi_k}\big[s(model, X_{\pi_k}, y)\big] \tag{1}$$

Standard error of the importance estimate across the \(R\) repeats, reported alongside Imp(k) to show how noisy each field's estimate is:

$$\text{SE}(k) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{R}}\, \text{std}_r\!\left(s(model, X, y) - s(model, X_{\pi_k}^{(r)}, y)\right) \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance (core/ml_engines.py::permutation_feature_importance), fitting the chosen model once via the same build_cv_estimator dispatcher used by Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator and ML Model Comparison, so model configuration is identical across all three tools.
3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
TARGETAny Field——Target field
FEATURESNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldExplanatory fields
TASK_TYPEEnumRegressionRegression / ClassificationPrediction task type
MODELEnumRandom ForestRF / Extra Trees / GBM(sklearn) / SVM / MLPModel to explain

4. Output Description

HTML report — a ranked horizontal bar chart of each field's mean importance, followed by a table with the standard deviation across repeats and the baseline (unshuffled) score.

Report includes: a ranked bar chart (inline SVG, no external dependency) of mean importance by field, drawn directly from the same sorted values shown in the table below it.

5. Interpretation Guide
A wide standard deviation across repeats means the estimate is itself noisy — raise Number of repeats. A near-zero or negative importance means the model did not rely on that field; consider dropping it and checking whether the remaining ranking stays stable. This tool does not cross-validate — pair with Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator for an honest accuracy figure alongside the ranking.

When to prefer this over MDI or gain-based native importances. Use Permutation Feature Importance whenever the model in question either has no native importance (SVM, MLP) or when a native importance ranking (Random Forest's MDI, XGBoost's gain) is suspected of being biased — for example, toward high-cardinality continuous fields. Because it directly measures score degradation on the metric the analyst actually cares about (R2 or accuracy), it is the most defensible ranking to present when the audience will ask "why should I trust this ranking."

See also: SHAP Global Feature Importance · Partial Dependence Report

Breiman, L. (2001). "Random Forests." Machine Learning 45(1): 5–32. DOI: 10.1023/A:1010933404324

Fisher, A., Rudin, C. & Dominici, F. (2019). "All Models Are Wrong, but Many Are Useful: Learning a Variable's Importance by Studying an Entire Class of Prediction Models Simultaneously." Journal of Machine Learning Research 20(177): 1–81.

Partial Dependence Report

partial_dependence_report
Fits a model, then shows how the average prediction changes as one chosen field is swept across its observed range while every other field is held at each record's actual value and the results averaged — the direction-of-effect question feature importances and SHAP summaries do not answer on their own.
1. Theoretical Background

Friedman's marginal-effect construction. Friedman (2001) introduced the Partial Dependence Plot alongside Gradient Boosting as a way to visualize a fitted model's average marginal effect for one (or two) features, integrating out — by averaging over the observed joint distribution — the influence of every other feature. This gives an "all else held at its observed values" curve, distinct from and complementary to a permutation-based importance score: PDP shows the shape and direction of a relationship, not just its overall magnitude.

The correlated-features caveat. Partial dependence assumes the swept field is reasonably independent of the other explanatory fields. When it is strongly correlated with another selected field, the curve evaluates combinations of values that may never actually occur together in reality, which can produce a misleading shape — a limitation Friedman himself notes and one Goldstein et al.'s (2015) Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) extension was designed to help diagnose by showing per-record curves instead of only their average.

Complementary to, not redundant with, SHAP. Partial dependence and SHAP Spatial Attribution Map both describe a field's effect, but at different resolutions: this tool answers "on average across the whole study area, how does the outcome change as this field changes," a single curve; SHAP's spatial map answers "at this specific location, how much did this field push the prediction," a per-record value that can and does vary by location even for the same field value, once interactions with other fields are accounted for. A field can show a strongly increasing partial dependence curve overall while still having sharply different SHAP contributions in different subregions — the two views genuinely answer different questions and are best read together, not as alternatives to pick one from.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Partial dependence of the model \(\hat{f}\) on feature \(x_S\) (fixed value \(v\)), averaged over the observed distribution of the remaining fields \(x_C\):

$$\text{PD}(v) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{f}(x_S=v,\, x_{C}^{(i)}) \tag{1}$$

Individual Conditional Expectation curve for one record \(i\) (Goldstein et al., 2015) — PD(v) above is exactly the average of these across all records; comparing the two reveals whether that average is representative:

$$\text{ICE}_i(v) = \hat{f}(x_S=v,\, x_C^{(i)}) \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.inspection.partial_dependence (core/ml_engines.py::partial_dependence_report). For classification, the curve shows the effect on the predicted probability of the first class in sorted class-label order (consistent with the class-selection convention used throughout this group's SHAP tools).
3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
TARGETAny Field——Target field
FEATURESNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldModel context fields
PD_FIELDNumeric Field—Must be in FEATURESField to sweep
TASK_TYPEEnumRegressionRegression / ClassificationPrediction task type
MODELEnumRandom ForestRF / Extra Trees / GBM(sklearn) / SVM / MLPModel to explain
GRID_POINTSInteger205–200Number of sweep points
4. Output Description

HTML report only — a table of PD_FIELD value versus average predicted outcome.

5. Interpretation Guide
Read the curve's shape (increasing, decreasing, U-shaped, plateauing) as the field's marginal relationship with the outcome, not as a causal claim. Check correlations between explanatory fields before trusting the curve if the swept field is likely correlated with another selected field. A flat curve means the model's predictions barely change with this field once the other fields are already in the model — not necessarily that the field is unrelated to the outcome on its own.

A non-monotonic (U-shaped or hump-shaped) curve is itself a finding. Unlike a linear regression coefficient, which forces a single constant direction of effect, a tree-based or boosting model's partial dependence curve can show the outcome first falling then rising (or the reverse) across a field's range — a genuine non-linear planning relationship (e.g. transit accessibility helping up to a point before a different effect like congestion offsets it) that OLS or GLR would report as a weak, washed-out linear coefficient. A curve like this is a specific, concrete reason to prefer a non-linear model over a linear one for the outcome in question.

See also: SHAP Spatial Attribution Map · SHAP Local Explanation

Goldstein, A., Kapelner, A., Bleich, J. & Pitkin, E. (2015). "Peeking Inside the Black Box: Visualizing Statistical Learning with Plots of Individual Conditional Expectation." Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 24(1): 44–65. DOI: 10.1080/10618600.2014.907095

ML Model Comparison (Leaderboard)

ml_model_comparison
Runs Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation for every selected model family on the same target and explanatory fields, then ranks them by mean out-of-sample score in a single leaderboard — an apples-to-apples comparison instead of eyeballing separate reports from each tool.
1. Theoretical Background

Model selection by cross-validated score comparison is standard machine-learning practice (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, 2009, Ch. 7); this tool applies it specifically with the spatially blocked folds from Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator, so the comparison inherits the same protection against spatial-autocorrelation leakage rather than comparing models on an optimistic, randomly-shuffled score. Only the scikit-learn Gradient Boosting engine is included in the comparison (no xgboost/lightgbm dependency required just to see which model FAMILY wins) — once boosting wins, the dedicated Gradient Boosting tools offer the XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost engines for the final fit.

Why a leaderboard is a safer starting point than picking a favorite model. It is tempting to always reach for whichever model performed best on a previous, unrelated dataset — but the "no free lunch" observation in machine learning (Wolpert & Macready, 1997) is precisely that no single model dominates across all problems; which family wins depends on the specific data-generating process behind each dataset. Running this leaderboard at the start of any new predictive analysis, rather than assuming Random Forest (or any other favorite) will win again, costs little relative to the risk of quietly leaving accuracy on the table with an unjustified default choice.

2. Mathematical Formulation

For each selected model \(m\), the leaderboard reports \(\bar{s}_m \pm \sigma_m\), the mean and standard deviation of the per-fold score from Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator (equations in that entry). Models are ranked by \(\bar{s}_m\) descending.

Implementation note. Implemented in algorithms/alg_ml_model_comparison.py, reusing core/ml_engines.py::spatial_kfold_evaluate directly for each candidate model rather than duplicating cross-validation logic — the leaderboard and the standalone CV evaluator are guaranteed to agree on any model run through both.

5. Interpretation Guide
A leaderboard where every model scores within one standard deviation of each other means model choice barely matters for this dataset — in that case, prefer the simplest or most interpretable option (Random Forest) over a marginally higher-ranked but harder-to-explain one. A winning model that leads the runner-up by more than its own standard deviation is a reasonably clear result.

The leaderboard picks a family, not a final production model. Once a family wins (say, Gradient Boosting), still run the dedicated tool for that family with its own engine choice (scikit-learn/XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost), hyperparameter tuning, and full diagnostic report (residual autocorrelation check, SHAP explanation) rather than treating the leaderboard's built-in default settings as the finished analysis — this tool is a fast screening step, not a substitute for the fuller workflow the winning model's dedicated tool provides.

⚖️

SHAP Global Feature Importanceoptional

shap_global_importance
Computes SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values — a game-theoretic attribution that splits each prediction into per-field contributions summing exactly to (prediction − average prediction) — and averages their absolute magnitude across records for a global importance ranking that is internally consistent with the per-record explanations in SHAP Spatial Attribution Map and SHAP Local Explanation Report.
1. Theoretical Background

Shapley values, borrowed from cooperative game theory. Lundberg and Lee (2017) proposed SHAP as a unification of several earlier local-explanation methods (LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation) under a single game-theoretic foundation: Shapley's (1953) solution to the problem of fairly dividing a cooperative game's payout among its players, applied here by treating each explanatory field as a "player" contributing to the "payout" of one prediction. The Shapley value for a field is its average marginal contribution across every possible order in which fields could be "added" to the prediction, which is the unique attribution satisfying a specific, mathematically desirable set of fairness axioms (efficiency, symmetry, dummy, additivity) — no other attribution scheme satisfies all four simultaneously.

Why this over Permutation Feature Importance. Permutation importance answers "how much does the model's overall SCORE drop if this field is scrambled" — a useful but coarser question than SHAP's "how much did this field contribute to THIS prediction, fairly accounting for interactions with other fields." Averaging SHAP's per-record, per-field contributions gives a global ranking, but the same underlying values also support the per-record map (SHAP Spatial Attribution Map) and single-record breakdown (SHAP Local Explanation Report) this ranking alone cannot provide.

Approximated, not exact, for non-tree models. The efficiency axiom (eq. 2) holds exactly for TreeExplainer's output; for the black-box SVM/MLP path, SHAP values are estimated by sampling coalitions rather than computed via the tree-structure shortcut, so they carry sampling variance and the additivity in equation 2 holds only approximately. Explainable Boosting Machine Regression/Classification offers a genuinely exact, sampling-free alternative to this tool specifically for its own glass-box model family, at the cost of applying only to that one model rather than to any model in this group the way SHAP does.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Shapley value for field \(k\) (all field subsets \(S\) not containing \(k\), model \(f\), background expectation \(\mathbb{E}\)):

$$\phi_k = \sum_{S \subseteq \{1,\dots,p\}\setminus\{k\}} \frac{|S|!\,(p-|S|-1)!}{p!}\Big[f_S(x_{S\cup\{k\}}) - f_S(x_S)\Big] \tag{1}$$

Additivity (efficiency axiom) — every prediction decomposes exactly:

$$f(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(X)] + \sum_{k=1}^{p} \phi_k(x) \tag{2}$$

Global importance (this tool's headline output):

$$\text{Imp}(k) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} |\phi_k(x_i)| \tag{3}$$
Implementation note. Tree-based models (Random Forest, Extra Trees, Gradient Boosting) use shap.TreeExplainer, which computes exact Shapley values in low-order polynomial time by exploiting tree structure (Lundberg, Erion & Lee, 2018) rather than the exponential brute-force sum of equation 1. SVM and MLP use shap.Explainer with a background sample, treating the model as a black-box function — slower, so Max rows to explain caps runtime by explaining a random subsample rather than every record on large layers (core/xai_engines.py::compute_shap_values).

MAX_ROWSInteger20020–5000Max rows to explain
4. Output Description

HTML report only — a table of mean |SHAP value| per field, sorted descending.

5. Interpretation Guide
A ranking based on a small subsample (n_explained well below the complete-record count) carries more noise — raise Max rows to explain if runtime allows. Ranking disagreement with Permutation Feature Importance on the same fields is worth investigating rather than dismissing either result. Follow up with SHAP Spatial Attribution Map to see where each field's contribution is concentrated geographically.

Choosing between SHAP and EBM for explanation. If the underlying model is one of Random Forest, Extra Trees, Gradient Boosting, SVM, or MLP, SHAP is the only exact-or-near-exact explanation tool available for it in this group. If interpretability is the primary goal and the small accuracy trade-off is acceptable, fitting Explainable Boosting Machine Regression/Classification directly instead — rather than fitting a black-box model and then explaining it with SHAP — sidesteps the approximation question entirely.

See also: SHAP Spatial Attribution Map · SHAP Local Explanation · Permutation Feature Importance · Explainable Boosting Machine Regression

🗺️

SHAP Spatial Attribution Mapflagship

shap_spatial_map
This plugin's distinctive way to use SHAP: rather than only a summary table, writes each explanatory field's SHAP contribution back onto the map as a new column per field (shap_<field>) — so any field can be symbolized to see WHERE it pushes the prediction up or down, not just how much it matters on average.
1. Theoretical Background

Global importance can hide large spatial variation. A field that matters strongly in one district and not at all in another averages out, in SHAP Global Feature Importance, to a moderate score that reveals nothing about WHERE it matters. Because every SHAP value in equation 1 (SHAP Global Feature Importance) is already computed per-record, nothing needs recomputing to expose that spatial pattern — this tool simply writes the already-computed per-record, per-field values back onto the source geometry as attribute columns, turning a black-box model's internal reasoning into a set of ordinary, symbolizable map layers. This is often the more actionable view for planning work than any single summary number, and it is the reason this tool exists as a distinct entry from SHAP Global Feature Importance rather than a report-only variant.

Reading a mapped SHAP field. Because SHAP values are signed and additive (equation 2 in SHAP Global Feature Importance), a diverging color ramp centered on zero is the correct symbology: positive shap_<field> values push a record's prediction above the average (shap_base), negative values push it below. A field with a coherent spatial pattern when mapped this way — not scattered noise — is genuinely operating differently across the study area, a pattern a global ranking alone cannot reveal.

Why every field gets its own column instead of one combined "top driver" column. A tempting simplification would be a single mapped field showing, per record, which explanatory field contributed most — but that discards magnitude and sign information, and different fields can be the top driver in adjoining records for reasons that look like noise on such a map even when each individual shap_<field> surface is smooth and coherent. Exporting the full set of per-field columns costs a little more storage and requires the analyst to choose which field to symbolize, but preserves the information a single "winner" column would destroy.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Uses the identical Shapley-value formulation as SHAP Global Feature Importance (equations 1–2 there); this tool's only addition is writing the per-record \(\phi_k(x_i)\) values to the output layer instead of (or alongside) averaging them into a single ranking.

Implementation note. Shares core/xai_engines.py::compute_shap_values with the other two SHAP tools. Records beyond Max rows to explain are not sampled and have shap_used = 0 with NULL SHAP columns — always check shap_used before concluding a field has "no effect" somewhere on the map, since it may simply not have been sampled there.

5. Interpretation Guide
Symbolize one field at a time. Each record's prediction equals shap_base plus the sum of ALL its shap_<field> values — trying to read several mapped fields together defeats the purpose of the decomposition. Use a diverging ramp centered on zero. Cross-check a striking spatial pattern with Model Residual Spatial Autocorrelation Check to confirm the underlying model has not simply left unexplained spatial structure that happens to correlate with the mapped field.

A mapped SHAP pattern describes the model, not necessarily causation. A clean spatial gradient in shap_road_density, for instance, shows that the fitted model relies on road_density differently across the study area — it does not by itself establish that road density causally drives the outcome in those areas, since the model may be picking up a genuine causal effect, a confound correlated with road density, or an artifact of how the training data happened to be distributed. Treat a striking mapped pattern as a strong lead for further investigation (a targeted OLS/GWR check on the pattern's subregion, or domain knowledge review) rather than a finished causal claim.

See also: SHAP Global Feature Importance · SHAP Local Explanation · Model Residual Spatial Autocorrelation Check

SHAP Local Explanation Reportoptional

shap_local_explanation
Computes a full SHAP breakdown for exactly one record, identified by its QGIS feature ID: every field's signed contribution, ranked by magnitude, summing with the base value to that record's prediction.
1. Theoretical Background

This is the same additive decomposition (equation 2, SHAP Global Feature Importance) as the other two SHAP tools, applied to a single targeted record instead of a sample or the full dataset — the canonical "waterfall" presentation of a SHAP explanation from Lundberg and Lee's (2017) original paper, where each field's bar shows how much it pushed the prediction above or below the average, in order from largest to smallest contribution.

The natural companion to DiCE Counterfactual Explanation, not a substitute for it. This tool answers "what drove this record's prediction" — a backward-looking, attribution question. DiCE Counterfactual Explanation (classification targets only) answers the forward-looking complement: "what would need to change for a different outcome." Running both on the same record gives a complete picture: this tool identifies which fields the model currently leans on, and DiCE shows whether nudging those same fields (or different ones entirely) would actually flip the outcome — the two do not always agree, and when they disagree it usually means the record sits in a region where the model's decision boundary is shaped by field interactions this single-record SHAP breakdown does not fully expose on its own.

Why the background sample still matters for a single-record explanation. Even though only one record is explained, its SHAP values are computed relative to a background distribution representing "typical" field values (equation 1's coalition sums, SHAP Global Feature Importance) — drawn from the full complete-case dataset, not just the one record. This means the same record's SHAP breakdown can differ depending on what population it is being explained relative to: a parcel that looks unusual against a citywide background may look unremarkable against a background restricted to its own district, and vice versa. This tool always uses the full input layer as background, matching the other two SHAP tools for consistency.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Identical to equations 1–2 in SHAP Global Feature Importance, evaluated at a single record \(x_i\) and reported in full rather than averaged or aggregated.

Implementation note. Reuses core/xai_engines.py::compute_shap_values with an explicit_rows override targeting exactly the requested feature ID's row (rather than a random subsample), so the background sample for non-tree models is still drawn from the full dataset while only the one requested record is explained — keeping runtime proportional to one prediction, not the whole layer.

Positive contributions push the prediction up (or toward the explained class); negative push it down (or away). Use after SHAP Spatial Attribution Map or the Identify tool points to a specific feature worth understanding — an outlier prediction, a surprising high-confidence classification, or a record a stakeholder is asking about specifically.

Explaining a stakeholder-facing decision. When a specific record's prediction needs to be defended to a stakeholder (why was this parcel flagged, why was this district scored the way it was), this tool's ranked, signed field list is the most direct artifact this plugin can produce for that conversation — far more concrete than a global importance ranking, which cannot speak to any one record specifically. Pair with the actual field values for that record (visible in the attribute table) so each SHAP contribution can be read alongside the underlying number that produced it.

DiCE Counterfactual Explanationoptional

dice_counterfactual_explanation
Searches for the smallest, most diverse field changes to one specific record that would flip a classifier's predicted class — Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (Mothilal, Sharma & Tan, ACM FAT* 2020). The action-oriented complement to SHAP Local Explanation's "what drove this" view: "what would have to be different."
1. Theoretical Background

Feature attribution versus recourse. SHAP Local Explanation Report decomposes an existing prediction into per-field contributions — a backward-looking account of what the model already did. Counterfactual explanation, introduced as a legal and technical framing by Wachter, Mittelstadt & Russell (2017, "Counterfactual Explanations Without Opening the Black Box"), asks a forward-looking, action-oriented question instead: what is the smallest change to this specific record's fields that would have produced a different, desired outcome? For a parcel classified as unlikely to redevelop, that answer is directly actionable in a way a SHAP contribution ranking alone is not — it names a concrete lever, not just a cause.

Diversity, not just proximity. A single nearest counterfactual can be misleading — it may happen to move a field that is not actually changeable in practice, when another, equally minimal counterfactual moving a different field would have worked just as well. Mothilal, Sharma & Tan (2020) formalized this by optimizing for a set of counterfactuals simultaneously, trading off three objectives: each counterfactual must (a) actually flip the prediction to the desired class, (b) stay close to the original record (proximity — small, plausible edits), and (c) stay far from the other counterfactuals in the set (diversity — different edits, so the set as a whole surveys distinct, independent levers rather than trivial variations on one).

Actionability via immutability constraints. Not every field a model uses can genuinely be changed by a planning decision — a parcel's legal zoning code or a fixed lot-geometry attribute is not a lever, even if the model finds it predictive. This tool's Immutable fields parameter removes such fields from the search entirely, so every field named in a returned counterfactual is, by construction, one the analyst chose to treat as changeable.

2. Mathematical Formulation

DiCE's joint objective over a set of \(k\) candidate counterfactuals \(\{c_1,\ldots,c_k\}\) for query point \(x\), desired class \(y^*\) (\(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\) balance the three terms):

$$\min_{c_1,\ldots,c_k} \; \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \text{yloss}(f(c_i), y^*) \;+\; \frac{\lambda_1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \text{dist}(c_i, x) \;-\; \lambda_2\, \text{dpp\_diversity}(c_1,\ldots,c_k) \tag{1}$$

Diversity term, a determinantal-point-process style measure over the pairwise distance kernel \(K_{ij} = 1/(1+\text{dist}(c_i,c_j))\) (larger when counterfactuals are more spread out):

$$\text{dpp\_diversity} = \det(K) \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Wraps dice_ml's random-sampling method (core/ml_engines.py::fit_dice_counterfactuals) around whichever classifier from this group's Model parameter is selected, fit fresh on the layer's complete records. Immutable fields are removed from dice_ml's features_to_vary list entirely, not merely penalized, so they cannot appear changed in any returned counterfactual.
3. Parameters

TARGETAny Field—≥ 2 distinct classesClass label field

4. Output Description

This tool produces an HTML report only (no output vector layer, since it explains one record, not the whole layer): for each of the N_COUNTERFACTUALS returned, the fields that changed, their original and counterfactual values, and the class the counterfactual would produce.

5. Interpretation Guide
A counterfactual is only as trustworthy as the classifier behind it. Cross-check the chosen Model's cross-validated accuracy (Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator) before treating any counterfactual as a real planning lever — a counterfactual generated from an inaccurate model is not a reliable recommendation, however small the suggested edit looks.

Reading the returned set as a whole, not just the first result. If every one of the N_COUNTERFACTUALS proposes changing the same one or two fields, that convergence is itself informative — those fields likely matter most for this record's classification. If the set instead disagrees sharply about which fields to move, treat the model's decision boundary near this record as genuinely ambiguous rather than picking one counterfactual as "the" answer.

See also: SHAP Local Explanation Report · Partial Dependence Report · Spatial k-Fold CV Evaluator

⚖️

Explainable Boosting Machine Regression (EBM)optional

ebm_regression
Fits a glass-box generalized additive model (Lou, Caruana & Gehrke, KDD 2012; Microsoft's InterpretML implementation) whose per-field contribution to every prediction is exact — read directly off the fitted model, not approximated by sampling the way SHAP explains a black-box model. Requires the optional interpret package.
1. Theoretical Background

Generalized additive models, learned by boosting. A classical generalized additive model (GAM; Hastie & Tibshirani, 1990) writes the prediction as a sum of independent per-field shape functions, \(F(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_j f_j(x_j)\) — fully additive, so each field's effect can be plotted and read in isolation, unlike a tree ensemble's interacting splits. Lou, Caruana & Gehrke (2012) showed each \(f_j\) can be learned by gradient boosting itself: fit one shallow tree per field per round, cycling round-robin across all fields with a very low learning rate, so no single field's shape function races ahead and locks in before the others are fit. The result keeps a GAM's full interpretability while matching much of the accuracy of an uninterpretable ensemble on many tabular problems — Random Forest and Gradient Boosting effectively trade a GAM's transparency for the added flexibility of splits that combine fields; EBM keeps the transparency by construction and lets the round-robin boosting procedure recover as much of that missing flexibility as an additive structure allows.

Exact contributions, not sampled ones. Because the fitted model literally is a sum of per-field functions, \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \sum_j f_j(x_j)\), the contribution of field \(j\) to any single prediction is simply \(f_j(x_j)\) — a direct table lookup, computed once at fit time. SHAP, by contrast, must approximate a Shapley-value decomposition of an arbitrary opaque model via Monte Carlo sampling over feature coalitions, which is powerful (it works on any model) but is fundamentally an estimate with sampling variance. EBM's contributions carry no such variance; the same input always yields the same exact contribution.

Interactions disabled by design in this tool. EBM's full form (GA2M) also supports a small number of automatically-selected pairwise interaction terms, \(f_{jk}(x_j, x_k)\), which typically improve accuracy further. This tool disables them (interactions=0) so every model term maps 1:1 onto an explanatory field — keeping the exported per-record ebm_<field> columns unambiguous, at the cost of the small accuracy gain interactions would otherwise add.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Fully additive prediction (intercept \(\beta_0\) plus one shape function per field):

$$\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} f_j(x_j) \tag{1}$$

Each \(f_j\) is itself a sum of shallow boosted trees fit only on field \(j\), across \(M\) round-robin cycles (\(\nu\)=learning rate):

$$f_j(x_j) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \nu \cdot h_{j,m}(x_j) \tag{2}$$

Exact contribution of field \(j\) to prediction \(i\), reported directly as ebm_<field>:

$$\text{contrib}_{i,j} = f_j(x_{i,j}) \tag{3}$$
Implementation note. Wraps interpret.glassbox.ExplainableBoostingRegressor with interactions=0; per-record contributions are read via the model's explain_local() API (core/ml_engines.py::fit_ebm_regressor). ebm_intercept plus the sum of the ebm_<field> columns for a record exactly reconstructs ebm_pred.
3. Parameters

FEATURESNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldExplanatory fields

4. Output Description

5. Interpretation Guide
Map an ebm_<field> column directly instead of running a separate SHAP tool. Because the contribution is exact and additive, mapping ebm_transit_score (for example) shows precisely where that field pushed predictions up or down across the study area — the same use case as SHAP Spatial Attribution Map, but without SHAP's sampling approximation or the need to fit a second model.

When EBM underperforms a full-interaction engine. If R2 here is notably lower than Gradient Boosting Regression on the same fields, the gap is a direct, quantified estimate of how much this dataset's relationship depends on interactions between fields — information the interactions-disabled EBM cannot represent by construction. A large gap is itself a useful finding: it means no purely additive model, however well-fit, can fully describe this outcome.

See also: SHAP Global Feature Importance · SHAP Spatial Attribution Map · Gradient Boosting Regression (scikit-learn) · Spatial k-Fold CV Evaluator

Explainable Boosting Machine Classification (EBM)optional

ebm_classification
The classification counterpart of Explainable Boosting Machine Regression: the same glass-box additive model and exact-contribution mechanism, here predicting a binary class as a sum of per-field log-odds contributions. Requires the optional interpret package.
1. Theoretical Background

Lou, Caruana & Gehrke's (2012) additive-boosting mechanism (see Explainable Boosting Machine Regression) applies to classification via a logistic link: the model is additive on the log-odds scale, \(\text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \sum_j f_j(x_j)\), and each field's exact contribution is a log-odds shift toward or away from the positive class rather than a shift in the raw target's units.

Scoped to binary targets. Multiclass EBM produces a separate set of per-field contributions for each class simultaneously, which does not fit this tool's one-column-per-field export design. This tool therefore requires the target field to have exactly two classes; for three or more classes, use Random Forest Classification or a Gradient Boosting engine, paired with SHAP Global Feature Importance for an explanation.

Log-odds contributions are additive; probability contributions are not. Because the model is additive on the log-odds scale, not the probability scale, an ebm_<field> value cannot be read as "this field added N percentage points of probability" - the sigmoid link that converts log-odds to probability is non-linear, so the same log-odds contribution translates to a larger or smaller probability shift depending on where the record's baseline log-odds already sits (a shift near logit=0, i.e. probability near 0.5, moves probability more than the identical shift applied to an already-confident record near logit=+3 or -3). Two records with an identical ebm_road_density value can therefore see different probability impacts from it - this is expected, not an inconsistency, and is exactly the sigmoid's job.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Additive on the log-odds (logit) scale (intercept \(\beta_0\) plus one shape function per field, as in EBM Regression eq. 1, here feeding a logistic link):

$$\text{logit}(p_i) = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} f_j(x_{i,j}) \tag{1}$$

Converting back to a predicted probability (ebm_conf) via the sigmoid:

$$p_i = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\text{logit}(p_i)}} \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Wraps interpret.glassbox.ExplainableBoostingClassifier with interactions=0 (core/ml_engines.py::fit_ebm_classifier). ebm_intercept plus the sum of the ebm_<field> columns for a record, passed through a sigmoid, reconstructs the predicted probability for the second class in sorted label order.

Compare accuracy against Gradient Boosting Classification on the same fields; a large gap quantifies how much this target depends on interactions between fields that the interactions-disabled EBM cannot represent.

Reading ebm_<field> near logit zero versus far from it. Per the non-linear sigmoid link above, an ebm_<field> column is most directly interpretable as a probability-scale effect specifically for records whose overall predicted probability sits near 0.5 (logit near 0) — there, the sigmoid is nearly linear, so log-odds and probability shifts track closely. For records the model is already confident about (ebm_conf near 0 or 1), the same log-odds contribution corresponds to a much smaller probability shift; when presenting a mapped ebm_<field> column to a non-technical audience, note this rather than implying a constant "N percentage points per unit" rate everywhere on the map.

📡

Model Residual Spatial Autocorrelation Check

model_residual_autocorrelation
Fits a regression model from this group, then runs the same Global Moran's I test already used on GLR/SAR/SEM residuals elsewhere in this plugin, applied here to a machine-learning model's residuals — the check that a high R2 has not simply masked a real spatial process the explanatory fields do not capture.
1. Theoretical Background

Why ML models are not automatically exempt from this check. Residual spatial autocorrelation testing is standard practice for linear spatial regression (Anselin, 1988) precisely because OLS assumes independent errors, an assumption spatial data routinely violates. Tree ensembles and other ML models make no such explicit independence assumption, which can create a false sense that the check is unnecessary for them — but if none of the explanatory fields carry location information (distance-to-center, adjacency, coordinates themselves), a machine-learning model can reach a high in-sample R2 by fitting the available features closely while still leaving a real, unmodeled spatial process in its residuals. The same Moran's I test that flags this for linear models flags it here too.

What "fix" actually means for an ML model versus a linear one. For OLS, a significant residual Moran's I typically leads to a Spatial Lag or Spatial Error model that explicitly represents the spatial dependence structure. Tree ensembles and boosting have no equivalent spatially-structured-error extension available in this plugin, so the practical response for an ML model is different: add explanatory fields that carry the missing location signal directly (distance-to-center, a spatial-lag of the target itself, coordinate fields), refit, and re-run this check — the model does not need a spatial-error term if the spatial pattern is instead captured as an ordinary predictive feature.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Identical Global Moran's I formulation as used for GLR/SAR/SEM residual diagnostics elsewhere in this manual (see Global Moran's I), applied to \(e_i = y_i - \hat{f}(x_i)\), the chosen model's in-sample residuals, with the same row-standardized queen/KNN weights construction.

Implementation note. Reuses core/analysis_diagnostics.py::residual_spatial_autocorrelation_summary and the shared weights-building helper (core/weights.py::build_weights_matrix) directly — the identical code path Generalized Linear Regression's residual diagnostic uses — rather than reimplementing the Moran's I computation for this tool.
3. Parameters

5. Interpretation Guide
Do not trust a high-R2 ML model on spatial data until this comes back clean. A significant positive Moran's I (p < 0.05) means real spatial signal is being missed — add a distance-to-center or spatial-lag field and refit, or switch to a model built to account for spatial structure directly (GWR, MGWR, Spatial Lag/Error Regression, group 05).

Run this before, not only after, a model is finalized. Because this check reuses the exact fitting pipeline as every other tool in this group (same complete-case extraction, same model dispatcher), it costs little to run routinely on any ML fit that will inform a planning decision — treat it as a standard step alongside Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator, not a special diagnostic reserved for when results already look suspicious.

See also: SHAP Spatial Attribution Map · Global Moran's I · GWR
6. Literature

Prediction Uncertainty Map

prediction_uncertainty_map
Maps a bagging ensemble's confidence in its own predictions, using the spread of individual trees' predictions around their mean as an uncertainty proxy — available only for Random Forest and Extra Trees, the two ensembles where every member saw a different bootstrap resample.
1. Theoretical Background

Ensemble disagreement as an uncertainty proxy. Because every tree in a bagging ensemble trained on a different bootstrap resample, the spread of their individual predictions at a given point is informative: where the trees agree closely, the ensemble is confident; where they disagree widely, the region is likely sparse in training data or represents an unusual combination of explanatory-field values the forest has not seen consistently. This "ensemble variance" approach to uncertainty is a long-standing, well-established practical technique (formalized more rigorously as Quantile Regression Forests by Meinshausen, 2006) that requires no distributional assumption beyond the bagging structure itself. Gradient Boosting, SVM, and MLP have no equivalent per-member prediction spread without substantially more machinery, which is why this tool is deliberately scoped to the two bagging ensembles only.

A heuristic, not a calibrated guarantee. Meinshausen's (2006) Quantile Regression Forests formalizes this idea with a specific statistical construction, but the simplified version implemented here (raw per-tree spread and empirical percentiles) has no proven coverage guarantee the way Conformal Prediction Interval's jackknife+ intervals do — unc_low/unc_high should be read as "roughly how much the trees disagree," a useful and cheap signal, not a calibrated (1-alpha) interval with any specific target coverage rate. When a genuinely calibrated interval is needed (for a figure that will be reported with a stated confidence level), Conformal Prediction Interval is the more defensible tool, and it additionally works for every model in this group, not only Random Forest/Extra Trees.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Per-tree prediction spread (B trees):

$$\bar{y}(x) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x), \qquad s(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\big(T_b(x) - \bar{y}(x)\big)^2} \tag{1}$$

Rough interval from the empirical per-tree distribution:

$$[\,Q_{10}(x),\, Q_{90}(x)\,] = \text{10th/90th percentile of } \{T_b(x)\}_{b=1}^{B} \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Iterates model.estimators_ directly on a fitted RandomForestRegressor/ExtraTreesRegressor to collect every individual tree's prediction per record (core/ml_engines.py::prediction_uncertainty), rather than relying on any single summary statistic scikit-learn exposes by default.
3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
TARGETNumeric Field——Target field
FEATURESNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldExplanatory fields
MODELEnumRandom ForestRandom Forest / Extra TreesBagging ensemble
N_ESTIMATORSInteger20010–2000Number of trees
OUTPUTVector Layer——Output uncertainty layer
4. Output Description
FieldTypeDescription
unc_predDoubleMean prediction across all trees
unc_stdDoubleStandard deviation across trees (the uncertainty measure)
unc_lowDouble10th percentile of per-tree predictions
unc_highDouble90th percentile of per-tree predictions
5. Interpretation Guide
High unc_std areas are typically sparse training data or unusual field-value combinations, not random noise — prioritize field verification or additional data collection there before acting on predictions. Use unc_pred together with unc_std, never on its own, when making a decision from a prediction.

Choosing between this tool and Conformal Prediction Interval. Use this tool for a fast, free-with-the-fit uncertainty read specifically on a Random Forest or Extra Trees model, especially when the goal is exploratory (finding which areas need more data collection). Use Conformal Prediction Interval instead when the interval itself will be reported or acted on formally, when the model is anything other than Random Forest/Extra Trees, or when a specific, stated target coverage rate matters to the audience.

See also: Random Forest Regression · SHAP Local Explanation · Conformal Prediction Interval

Conformal Prediction Intervaloptional

conformal_prediction_interval
Computes distribution-free prediction intervals with a mathematically guaranteed marginal coverage rate, for any regression model in this group — not just the Random Forest/Extra Trees tree-vote spread Prediction Uncertainty Map relies on. Wraps MAPIE's jackknife+ conformal method (Barber, Candès, Ramdas & Tibshirani, 2021). Requires the optional mapie package.
1. Theoretical Background

A guarantee, not a heuristic. Prediction Uncertainty Map's tree-vote spread is a genuinely useful uncertainty signal, but it is a heuristic specific to bagging ensembles — nothing says the spread across trees is calibrated to any particular coverage rate, and the method has no meaning at all for SVM, MLP, or any non-ensemble model. Conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer, 2005) is different in kind: under only the assumption that the data is exchangeable (a weaker condition than the i.i.d. normal-error assumption behind a classical regression confidence interval), it produces intervals with a proven marginal coverage guarantee — across many predictions, at least \((1-\alpha)\) of the true values will fall inside their own interval, for any underlying model, regardless of whether that model's own uncertainty estimates are any good.

Jackknife+: cross-validation applied to calibration. The simplest form of conformal prediction (split conformal) sacrifices half the data purely to calibrate the interval width. Barber, Candès, Ramdas & Tibshirani (2021) introduced jackknife+ (and its cross-conformal generalization, used here) to recover that lost efficiency: the data is split into folds exactly as in k-fold cross-validation, a model is fit leaving each fold out in turn, and the leave-one-fold-out residuals across all folds are pooled to calibrate the final interval width — every record contributes to both fitting and calibration, at the cost of fitting the model N_FOLDS times instead of once.

What the guarantee does not promise. The coverage guarantee is marginal — averaged over all records — not conditional on any specific record's covariates. It is entirely possible for the interval to systematically undercover in one subregion of the study area and overcover in another while still averaging out to the target rate overall; a large gap between empirical and target coverage in this tool's report, or strong spatial structure in interval width, is a sign the exchangeability assumption may be strained by spatial autocorrelation specifically.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Jackknife+ interval for a new point, built from the \(N_{\text{FOLDS}}\) leave-one-fold-out models \(\hat{f}_{-k}\) and their held-out residuals \(R_i = |y_i - \hat{f}_{-k(i)}(x_i)|\):

$$\hat{C}(x) = \left[\, q^{-}_{\alpha}\!\left\{\hat{f}_{-k(i)}(x) - R_i\right\},\;\; q^{+}_{\alpha}\!\left\{\hat{f}_{-k(i)}(x) + R_i\right\} \,\right] \tag{1}$$

where \(q^{-}_{\alpha}\) and \(q^{+}_{\alpha}\) denote the \(\alpha\) and \((1-\alpha)\) empirical quantiles taken over all \(i\) in the calibration pool. Empirical coverage reported by this tool:

$$\widehat{\text{coverage}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\text{conf\_low}_i \le y_i \le \text{conf\_high}_i\right] \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Wraps mapie.regression.MapieRegressor with method="plus" around whichever model from this group's Model parameter is selected (core/ml_engines.py::fit_conformal_interval). Regression only — MAPIE's classification API produces variable-length prediction sets rather than fixed columns, which does not fit this tool's output schema.
3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
TARGETNumeric Field——Target field
FEATURESNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldExplanatory fields
MODELEnumRandom ForestAny Group 06 CV modelRegression model to calibrate
ALPHADouble0.10.01–0.5Miscoverage rate (interval targets 1−alpha coverage)
N_FOLDSInteger52–20Cross-conformal folds
OUTPUTVector Layer——Output layer with prediction intervals
4. Output Description
FieldTypeDescription
conf_predDoublePoint prediction from the conformal-calibrated model
conf_lowDoubleLower bound of the (1−alpha) prediction interval
conf_highDoubleUpper bound of the (1−alpha) prediction interval
conf_widthDoubleInterval width (conf_high − conf_low)
5. Interpretation Guide
Report the interval, not just conf_pred. When a prediction will inform a planning decision, conf_low–conf_high communicates how much to trust that specific record's prediction far better than a bare point value; a wide conf_width is itself a finding, not noise to discard.

Reading the empirical-versus-target coverage gap. The reported empirical coverage is computed in-sample and is therefore optimistic for the same structural reason every in-sample metric in this group is; treat a close match to the target as a mild positive signal, not proof the guarantee holds exactly. A large, persistent gap — especially paired with conf_width that visibly clusters by location — is a sign to check Model Residual Spatial Autocorrelation Check for the same model before trusting the intervals in a specific subregion.

See also: Prediction Uncertainty Map · Model Residual Spatial Autocorrelation Check · Spatial k-Fold CV Evaluator
6. Literature

Barber, R.F., Candès, E.J., Ramdas, A. & Tibshirani, R.J. (2021). "Predictive Inference with the Jackknife+." Annals of Statistics 49(1): 486–507. DOI: 10.1214/20-AOS1965

Vovk, V., Gammerman, A. & Shafer, G. (2005). Algorithmic Learning in a Random World. New York: Springer. ISBN 978-0-387-00152-4 — Foundational conformal prediction text.

Romano, Y., Patterson, E. & Candès, E. (2019). "Conformalized Quantile Regression." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32: 3543–3553.
