TabPFN Regression (Tabular Foundation Model)optional

tabpfn_regression
Fits a zero-shot regression prediction with TabPFN v2 (Hollmann et al., Nature, 2025): a transformer pretrained once, offline, on millions of synthetic tabular problems, performing in-context learning at call time rather than a per-dataset training loop. Requires the optional tabpfn package and, on first use, an internet connection to download pretrained weights.
1. Theoretical Background

Prior-fitted networks and in-context learning. Every other model in this group learns from your specific dataset: Random Forest grows trees on it, MLP updates weights against it over many epochs. Müller, Hollmann, Arango, Grabocka & Hutter (2022) introduced a different paradigm, the Prior-Fitted Network (PFN): a transformer is trained exactly once, offline, on an enormous stream of synthetic datasets sampled from a structural-causal-model prior, learning to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive inference, \(p(y^{*}\mid x^{*}, D_{\text{train}})\), as a single, amortized forward pass. At inference time on a genuinely new dataset, no further training happens: the training table and the query rows are simply passed through the network together as a prompt, and the network's pretraining has already taught it "how to learn" from a table it has never seen — this is what "in-context learning" means here, borrowing the same mechanism that lets a large language model follow a new instruction from its prompt alone.

TabPFN v2. Hollmann et al. (2023) first demonstrated this approach specifically for tabular classification (TabPFN v1); Hollmann et al. (2025, published in Nature) extended it to regression and substantially scaled the pretraining prior and model capacity as TabPFN v2, reporting that it matched or outperformed tuned Gradient Boosting on a wide range of small-to-medium tabular benchmarks while fitting in seconds with no hyperparameter search at all — a genuinely novel result for a field where tree ensembles have dominated for over a decade (Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux, 2022, had specifically documented deep learning's continued struggle to beat GBMs on tabular data, making TabPFN's approach notable rather than simply another neural architecture).

A hard, published operating envelope. TabPFN's in-context mechanism processes the entire training table within the transformer's attention computation at inference time, which does not scale indefinitely: the published, supported envelope is up to 10,000 rows and 500 features. This tool enforces that ceiling explicitly, raising a clear error rather than letting the underlying library degrade silently or fail with an opaque internal error past the boundary.

2. Mathematical Formulation

The Bayesian posterior predictive TabPFN is pretrained to approximate, for query point \(x^{*}\) given the training table \(D\) (integrating over the prior's latent data-generating parameters \(\theta\)):

$$p(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, D) = \int p(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \theta)\, p(\theta \mid D) \, d\theta \tag{1}$$

Pretraining objective (offline, once, over synthetic prior draws \((D, x^{*}, y^{*}) \sim \text{prior}\); \(g_\phi\) is the transformer with parameters \(\phi\)):

$$\phi^{*} = \arg\min_{\phi} \; \mathbb{E}_{(D,x^{*},y^{*}) \sim \text{prior}} \left[-\log g_\phi(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, D)\right] \tag{2}$$
Implementation note. Wraps tabpfn.TabPFNRegressor (core/ml_engines.py::fit_tabpfn_regressor), which downloads and caches pretrained weights on first use. No hyperparameters are exposed because none exist to tune — the model performs zero gradient-descent steps on your data.
First-use licensing (Windows). TabPFN requires a one-time license acceptance before its first local inference call. TabPFN's own interactive browser-login prompt polls the console in a way Windows does not support for a non-socket standard input, so it cannot complete inside QGIS's embedded Python console — accept the license once outside QGIS instead: open ux.priorlabs.ai/account, log in or register, accept the license, copy the API key, then set it as a permanent Windows environment variable named TABPFN_TOKEN and restart QGIS. After that, TabPFN authenticates silently on every run with no browser prompt. Running without a cached token raises a clear message with these same steps rather than a raw error.
3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
TARGETNumeric Field——Target field
FEATURESNumeric Fields—1–500 fieldsExplanatory fields
OUTPUTVector Layer—≤ 10,000 complete recordsOutput predictions layer

tabpfn_predDoubleIn-context predicted value

tabpfn_usedInteger1 if used to fit and predict, 0 otherwise
5. Interpretation Guide
The newest and least field-tested engine here — treat it as a second opinion, not a default. TabPFN's benchmark performance is well documented on published, general-purpose tabular datasets, but it has far less accumulated track record on planning-domain data specifically than Random Forest or any Gradient Boosting engine. Cross-check its R2 against Gradient Boosting Regression on the same fields, and always confirm out-of-sample behavior with Spatial k-Fold Cross-Validation Evaluator before relying on it for a planning decision.

An unusually large R2 deserves scrutiny, not celebration. Because TabPFN has no hyperparameters to overfit in the conventional sense, an R2 that is markedly higher than every tree-based engine with no clear explanation is more often a sign of target leakage in the explanatory fields than of a genuinely superior fit — check for a field that encodes the target directly or near-directly before trusting the result.

See also: Gradient Boosting Regression (scikit-learn) · Permutation Feature Importance · Spatial k-Fold CV Evaluator

Hollmann, N., Müller, S., Purucker, L., Krishnakumar, A., Körfer, M., Hoo, S.B., Schirrmeister, R.T. & Hutter, F. (2025). "Accurate Predictions on Small Data with a Tabular Foundation Model." Nature 637: 319–326. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08328-6

Müller, S., Hollmann, N., Arango, S.P., Grabocka, J. & Hutter, F. (2022). "Transformers Can Do Bayesian Inference." International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

TabPFN Classification (Tabular Foundation Model)optional

tabpfn_classification
The classification counterpart of TabPFN Regression: the same pretrained, in-context-learning transformer (Hollmann et al., Nature, 2025), here predicting a categorical target with no per-dataset training loop and no hyperparameters to tune. Requires the optional tabpfn package and, on first use, an internet connection.
1. Theoretical Background

The in-context-learning mechanism described in TabPFN Regression applies directly to classification: TabPFN's pretraining prior includes synthetic classification tasks, so the same forward pass approximates a Bayesian posterior predictive class distribution, \(p(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, D)\), for a categorical \(y^{*}\) rather than a continuous one. TabPFN's pretrained classification head was built and validated for a bounded number of classes; this tool enforces that ceiling (10 classes) explicitly.

Why a 10-class ceiling specifically. TabPFN's classification head is not a generic softmax fit at inference time the way a neural network's output layer would be — it is itself part of what was pretrained, over synthetic classification tasks drawn from the same structural-causal-model prior as the regression version, with a bounded number of possible output classes baked into the pretrained architecture. This is a fundamentally different constraint from, say, scikit-learn's SVC needing more one-vs-one sub-models as classes grow (Support Vector Classification): TabPFN simply has no mechanism to represent an 11th class, regardless of dataset size or compute budget, until a future retrained version of the model expands that architecture.

Confidence and calibration on a model this new. Because TabPFN performs no gradient descent on the user's own data, tabpfn_conf reflects the pretrained model's posterior belief conditioned on the training table shown in-context — not a quantity fit or calibrated against this specific dataset the way, for instance, SVC's Platt-scaled probability is. Published benchmarking (Hollmann et al., 2025) reports TabPFN v2's calibration compares favorably to Gradient Boosting on general tabular benchmarks, but as with its raw accuracy, there is limited independent evidence of that calibration quality holding on planning-domain data specifically.

Implementation note. Wraps tabpfn.TabPFNClassifier (core/ml_engines.py::fit_tabpfn_classifier), which shares the row/feature envelope and first-use weight download of the regression engine, plus a 10-class ceiling.
First-use licensing (Windows). See TabPFN Regression's identical note above: on Windows, accept the license once at ux.priorlabs.ai/account and set a permanent TABPFN_TOKEN environment variable before running this tool in QGIS, since the library's own interactive browser-login prompt cannot complete inside QGIS's embedded console on Windows.

DBSCAN Density-Based Clustering

dbscan_clustering
Groups features into density-based clusters of arbitrary shape: a point belongs to a cluster if at least Min samples other points fall within Epsilon distance of it in standardized attribute space, clusters grow by chaining such neighborhoods, and unqualified points are labeled noise (cluster_id = -1) rather than forced into the nearest cluster.
1. Theoretical Background

Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu (1996) introduced DBSCAN as an alternative to centroid-based clustering (K-Means) that needs no predetermined cluster count and can recover clusters of arbitrary shape, not just roughly convex, similarly-sized ones. A point is "core" if at least MinPts points (including itself) fall within distance Epsilon; clusters form by chaining together core points and their neighbors, and points reachable by no core point are explicit noise — a structural difference from K-Means, which assigns every point to the nearest centroid regardless of how poorly it fits.

Noise as a first-class result, not a failure. Unlike Multivariate Clustering (K-Means), which forces every record into a cluster whether it belongs or not, DBSCAN's explicit noise label (cluster_id = -1) is often the more useful part of the output for a planning question framed around identifying outliers or exceptions — parcels that don't fit any coherent typology in the study area — rather than the clusters themselves. Mapping the noise points alone, on their own, is a legitimate and often revealing analysis in its own right.

2. Mathematical Formulation

\(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood and core-point condition:

$$N_\varepsilon(p) = \{q : d(p,q) \le \varepsilon\}, \qquad p \text{ is core} \iff |N_\varepsilon(p)| \ge \text{MinPts} \tag{1}$$

Density-reachability (clusters = maximal sets connected by chains of core points):

$$q \text{ reachable from } p \iff \exists\, p=p_1,\dots,p_n=q,\ p_{i+1}\in N_\varepsilon(p_i),\ p_i \text{ core} \tag{2}$$

Unlike K-Means, DBSCAN has no explicit objective function it minimizes globally — a cluster is simply a maximal connected component of the density-reachability graph implied by equations 1–2, which is what allows it to trace arbitrarily elongated or non-convex shapes a centroid-based method structurally cannot.

Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.cluster.DBSCAN after Z-score standardizing the selected fields (core/ml_engines.py::fit_dbscan), the same standardization convention as Multivariate Clustering (K-Means). Epsilon is therefore in standardized-space units, not the fields' original units.
3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
FIELDSNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldAnalysis fields (Z-score standardized)
EPSDouble0.750.01–20.0Neighborhood radius (standardized space)
MIN_SAMPLESInteger52–200Min points per neighborhood
OUTPUTVector Layer——Output clustered layer
4. Output Description
cluster_id — cluster index, or -1 for noise/outlier points
5. Interpretation Guide
Epsilon is the hardest parameter to set — start around 0.5–1.0 and adjust: too small produces almost all noise, too large merges everything into one cluster. A run with more than half the records labeled noise usually means Epsilon is too small or Min samples too high for this dataset's density. Use HDBSCAN instead when the study area plausibly mixes dense and sparse sub-areas that a single Epsilon cannot separate correctly.

A practical Epsilon-tuning routine. Rather than guessing, sort every point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbor (k = Min samples) and look for the "elbow" where this sorted distance curve bends sharply upward — the classic k-distance-graph heuristic from Ester et al.'s (1996) original paper. That elbow value is a reasonable Epsilon starting point specific to this dataset's density, rather than an arbitrary default carried over from a different layer.

See also: HDBSCAN Hierarchical Density Clustering · Multivariate Clustering (K-Means)
6. Literature

Ester, M., Kriegel, H.-P., Sander, J. & Xu, X. (1996). "A Density-Based Algorithm for Discovering Clusters in Large Spatial Databases with Noise." Proceedings of the 2nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 226–231. — The original DBSCAN paper.

🔷

HDBSCAN Hierarchical Density Clusteringsklearn ≥1.3

hdbscan_clustering
Groups features into density-based clusters like DBSCAN, but builds a hierarchy of clusters across every density level and extracts the most stable ones automatically, instead of using one fixed Epsilon radius everywhere — handling clusters of different densities in the same layer that a single-Epsilon DBSCAN run cannot separate correctly.
1. Theoretical Background

Campello, Moulavi and Sander (2013) reformulated DBSCAN's fixed-Epsilon density threshold as a hierarchy: build a dendrogram of clusters across every possible density level (via a mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, closely related to the SKATER regionalization tool's own MST construction), then select the set of clusters that persist the longest — the "most stable" clusters — as the final flat clustering. This removes DBSCAN's single-Epsilon assumption entirely, at some additional computational cost, and produces a per-point cluster membership PROBABILITY (cluster_prob) rather than only a hard 0/1 assignment.

One parameter instead of two, and what that trade buys. DBSCAN requires both Epsilon and Min samples to be tuned jointly, and the right Epsilon can differ by density region within the same layer. HDBSCAN needs only Min cluster size because it evaluates stability across every density level automatically rather than committing to one — the cost is purely computational (building the full hierarchy is more expensive than a single DBSCAN pass), which is negligible on typical planning-scale layers of a few thousand records or fewer.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Builds on DBSCAN's core-point and reachability definitions (equations 1–2 there) but replaces the fixed \(\varepsilon\) with a mutual-reachability distance \(d_{\text{mreach}}(a,b) = \max(\text{core}_k(a), \text{core}_k(b), d(a,b))\) evaluated across all scales, then extracts the flat clustering that maximizes total cluster stability (area under each cluster's persistence in the resulting hierarchy) — the Excess of Mass algorithm from Campello, Moulavi & Sander (2013).

Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.cluster.HDBSCAN, available since scikit-learn 1.3, after Z-score standardizing the selected fields (core/ml_engines.py::fit_hdbscan). On an older scikit-learn, this raises the standard optional-dependency error naming the required version.

What "Excess of Mass" actually selects for. Rather than picking the single most persistent cluster at one arbitrary cut through the density hierarchy, the Excess of Mass criterion selects, independently for each branch of the hierarchy, whichever level maximizes that branch's total stability — the sum, across the density range the cluster persists over, of how many points it contains at each level. This tends to favor clusters that are both large and long-lived over small clusters that briefly look tight at one particular density threshold, a property directly relevant when the goal is finding genuine planning typologies rather than incidental local density bumps.

3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
FIELDSNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldAnalysis fields (Z-score standardized)
MIN_CLUSTER_SIZEInteger52–1000Minimum points to count as a cluster
OUTPUTVector Layer——Output clustered layer
4. Output Description
cluster_id — cluster index, or -1 for noise · cluster_prob — membership strength (0–1) in the assigned cluster
5. Interpretation Guide
Min cluster size is more intuitive than DBSCAN's Epsilon — a literal minimum record count. Raise it to merge small clusters into noise or larger neighbors; lower it to allow smaller, tighter groups. Prefer this over DBSCAN whenever the study area plausibly mixes dense and sparse sub-areas, common in mixed urban/suburban planning datasets.

Reading cluster_prob alongside cluster_id. A record with cluster_id assigned but a low cluster_prob is a weak, borderline member of that cluster, not a confidently typical one — when reporting cluster characteristics or selecting representative examples of a cluster for a planning narrative, filter to high-cluster_prob records rather than treating every member as equally representative.

See also: DBSCAN Density-Based Clustering · Gaussian Mixture Model Clustering
6. Literature

Campello, R.J.G.B., Moulavi, D. & Sander, J. (2013). "Density-Based Clustering Based on Hierarchical Density Estimates." Advances in Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (PAKDD 2013), LNCS 7819: 160–172. DOI: 10.1007/978-3-642-37456-2_14 — The original HDBSCAN paper.

🎨

Gaussian Mixture Model Clustering

gmm_clustering
Groups features into K clusters by fitting K overlapping Gaussian (elliptical) distributions to standardized attribute space via expectation-maximization — allowing elongated, differently-sized, differently-oriented clusters and a soft probability of membership in every cluster, unlike K-Means' hard, roughly-spherical assignment.
1. Theoretical Background

Dempster, Laird and Rubin's (1977) Expectation-Maximization algorithm is the standard fitting method for mixture models: alternately compute each point's probability of belonging to each component (E-step) and update each component's mean/covariance/weight given those soft assignments (M-step), iterating to convergence on the likelihood. Because each component is a full (or constrained) Gaussian rather than a spherical centroid, GMM can represent elongated or correlated clusters K-Means structurally cannot, and — because assignment is inherently probabilistic — a point near two components' boundary shows genuine uncertainty (e.g. 0.55/0.45) rather than an artificially confident hard label.

K-Means as a special case, not a competitor to rule out first. K-Means (Multivariate Clustering) is mathematically the limiting case of a GMM with equal, spherical, fixed-size components — so GMM with Spherical covariance and equal component weights recovers something close to K-Means, while Full covariance recovers genuinely elliptical clusters K-Means cannot represent at all. This makes GMM strictly more flexible in principle; the practical trade-off is that Full covariance needs meaningfully more records per cluster to estimate its covariance matrix reliably, which is why Covariance Type is exposed as an explicit choice rather than always defaulting to the most flexible option.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Mixture density (K components, weights \(\pi_k\)):

$$p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k\, \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k) \tag{1}$$

E-step — posterior (responsibility) of component \(k\) for point \(i\):

$$\gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j}\pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_j,\Sigma_j)} \tag{2}$$

Model selection (lower is better; this tool prints both to the Processing log):

$$\text{BIC} = -2\ln\hat{L} + m\ln n, \qquad \text{AIC} = -2\ln\hat{L} + 2m \tag{3}$$
Implementation note. Wraps sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture after Z-score standardizing the selected fields (core/ml_engines.py::fit_gmm). Covariance type controls per-component shape flexibility (Full to Spherical); Full needs the most data per cluster to fit reliably, Spherical is closest to K-Means and most stable on small datasets.

EM finds a local, not global, optimum. Because the log-likelihood surface EM climbs is generally non-convex, different random initializations can converge to different local optima — the practical reason scikit-learn's default fits several random restarts internally and keeps the best. On a small or genuinely ambiguous dataset, re-running this tool can occasionally produce a different cluster assignment; treat a result that is unstable across repeated runs (rather than merely across different K or covariance-type choices) as a sign the data does not support a confident mixture-model decomposition at all, and consider HDBSCAN's density-based alternative instead.

3. Parameters
ParameterTypeDefaultConstraintsDescription
INPUTVector Layer—Any geometry typeInput vector layer
FIELDSNumeric Fields—≥ 1 fieldAnalysis fields (Z-score standardized)
N_COMPONENTSInteger32–30Number of components (K)
COVARIANCE_TYPEEnumFullFull / Tied / Diagonal / SphericalComponent shape flexibility
OUTPUTVector Layer——Output clustered layer
4. Output Description
cluster_id — highest-probability component · gmm_p0, gmm_p1, ... — per-component membership probability (one column per K)
5. Interpretation Guide
Run this tool at several K values and pick the one with the lowest BIC (printed to the log) rather than assuming more components is always better. A point with probability spread across two components sits near their boundary — a genuinely useful signal K-Means's hard assignment discards. Switch to a more constrained covariance type if the fit does not converge or looks unstable with few records.

BIC versus AIC when they disagree. BIC (Schwarz, 1978) penalizes model complexity more heavily than AIC as the record count grows, so it tends to favor a smaller K on typical planning-scale datasets — the more conservative, generally preferred criterion for this tool's default recommendation. If AIC and BIC favor different K values, that disagreement itself is informative: it usually means the "right" number of clusters is genuinely ambiguous for this dataset, and the choice should be settled by planning-domain interpretability (does each cluster correspond to a coherent, nameable typology) rather than by the numeric criterion alone.

See also: Multivariate Clustering (K-Means) · HDBSCAN Hierarchical Density Clustering

Methodological Notes

Spatial Weights Matrix

The spatial weights matrix W is the single most consequential modeling choice in spatial statistics. GeoStats Lab supports four weight specifications, each appropriate for different data geometries and analytical questions:

  • Queen contiguity — features sharing a boundary or a vertex are neighbors. Appropriate for polygon tessellations (census tracts, administrative units).
  • Rook contiguity — features sharing a boundary (but not only a vertex) are neighbors. More restrictive than Queen; appropriate when corner-touching polygons are not meaningfully adjacent.
  • K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) — each feature's K closest features (by centroid distance) are neighbors. Guarantees every feature has exactly K neighbors. Recommended when feature density varies, or for point data.
  • Distance Band — all features within a fixed distance threshold are neighbors. Appropriate when the spatial process has a known or theorized range. Use Calculate Distance Band (01) or Incremental Spatial Autocorrelation (02) to determine the threshold.
Row-Standardization

All weights are row-standardized (each row of W sums to 1) before use in spatial statistics. Row-standardization makes the spatial lag Wy interpretable as a local average of neighbors' values. The exception is distance-decay kernels in GWR/MGWR, where weights are used in their natural (non-standardized) form to preserve the distance gradient.

Coordinate Reference Systems

Distance-based methods (Distance Band, KNN, Ripley's K, GWR/MGWR with fixed kernels) assume Euclidean distances in map units. Always use a projected CRS (e.g., UTM, State Plane) for distance-based analyses. Geographic CRS (latitude/longitude) produce distorted distances that vary with latitude. Contiguity-based weights (Queen, Rook) are unaffected by the CRS. MGWR offers a spherical-distance option for longitude/latitude coordinates.

Multiple Testing and Inference

Local statistics (Gi*, LISA, Bivariate LISA) perform a separate hypothesis test at each feature. With N features, this means N simultaneous tests. The default significance threshold of p < 0.05 is not corrected for multiple comparisons. For conservative inference, consider a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold (p < 0.05/N) or use the permutation-based p-values from Bivariate LISA. The plugin reports uncorrected p-values and confidence bins; the analyst decides the appropriate significance level for their use case. See de Castro & Singer (2006) and Anselin (2019) for guidance on multiple-testing correction in LISA.

Software Provenance

GeoStats Lab implements its own NumPy-based engines for all core computations (Moran's I, Gi*, LISA, GWR, Ripley's K, SDE, clustering, Gini decomposition). Where optional libraries are used (MGWR via mgwr; SAR/SEM via spreg), the library name and version are reported in every output. This hybrid approach balances the reliability of hand-audited implementations for common methods with the power of community-vetted packages for advanced methods. All engines are exercised against the bundled QA datasets in automated smoke tests.
